Twenty-one people spoke.[2]Senator Ron Johnson@SenRonJohnsonWatch the entire roundtable here⬇️Senator Ron Johnson @SenRonJohnsonCOVID-19 Hospital Protocols: Real Stories from Real People5:40 PM · Oct 1, 2026 · 4.52K Views7 Replies · 41 Reposts · 85 LikesJohnson’s office describes what they said: remdesivir and ventilation “forced on patients as the only viable options,” ivermectin and monoclonal antibodies denied “even when rigid hospital protocols were failing,” families kept from dying relatives, and “callous comments by doctors and nurses to unvaccinated patients and their families.” These are people who watched what happened at the bedside, and several of them paid for saying so. They are owed more than four hours in a Senate office building.[2]📷A nurse who watched the roundtable wrote a post that Wall Street Apes circulated: “It was handed to us from the top down. Every hospital got the same treatment guidelines, guidelines that said in writing, not a mandate, but every hospital followed this like it was the law.”[3] She added the payment rules, the lockouts, the staff mandate and a legal shield that runs to 2029. “If you didn’t follow it, you were out.”She was right about almost all of it. We checked each claim against the Federal Register, the Congressional Record, CMS manuals, court files, lobbying disclosures and the drug company’s own filings. Then we asked the question underneath hers: who wrote these rules?Different hands wrote each layer: an NIH panel, HHS’s preparedness office, Congress and the Medicare agency, the Medicare agency again, the HHS Secretary, and each hospital’s own administration. The hospitals acted as if all of them did.
Six layers
The treatment guidelines. Written by a panel at the National Institutes of Health.[4]
The drug. The Department of Health and Human Services signed a deal with Gilead Sciences that governed who got remdesivir from July through September 2020 and recorded its price.[5]
The money. Congress wrote a 20 percent Medicare bonus on the payment for each COVID inpatient stay. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) added a second payment for stays that used remdesivir.[6, 7]
The visitors and the staff mandate. CMS wrote the nursing-home visitor ban and the staff vaccine mandate.[8, 9]
The legal shield. HHS declared COVID countermeasures immune from suit, and has extended the declaration to 31 December 2029.[10, 11]
The hospital’s own daily orders. This is the layer a nurse actually touches. A surgeon at the hospital that treated the first American COVID patient swears under penalty of perjury that his chief medical officer sent staff “weekly to daily directives” relaying CDC and CMS requirements for more than a year.[12]The NIH panel says its guidelines “should not be considered mandates.”[4] CMS’s own explainer for the 20 percent bonus says it is “not intended to grant rights or impose obligations.”[13] Hospitals followed the guidelines and the payment rules as if they were law. The surgeon, Dr. James P. Miller, swears that at Everett “it was understood that you would lose your job and/or license if you did not maintain compliance,” and that he was taught at a CMS-compliance conference that non-compliance “meant certain financial destruction and bankruptcy for that hospital or medical group.”[12]📷The rest of this article follows the layers one at a time, then the people who sat around the table when they were written.
The panel that wrote the treatment protocolThe panel began in March 2020 at the request of the White House Coronavirus Task Force, passed through the HHS Secretary to NIH. Anthony Fauci’s institute, NIAID, “initiated the formation” of it. The first guidelines went up on 21 April 2020.[4] Three co-chairs ran it: Roy Gulick of Weill Cornell, Cliff Lane of NIAID and Henry Masur of the NIH Clinical Center.[14, 15] Over four years it voted 438 times.[16]It never published how a single member voted. It never published a rule requiring a member to sit out a vote on a product made by a company that paid them. The only conflict-of-interest procedure on record is that the co-chairs reviewed disclosures twice a year “to determine suitability for membership,” and that panel leadership used them to decide whether a member should take part.[14, 4, 16]The disclosure tables show why that matters. In April 2020 eleven panel members listed a financial relationship with a drug company. Nine of the eleven listed Gilead, the maker of remdesivir: Aberg, Adimora, Baker, Bedimo, Daar, Gandhi, Glidden, Naggie and Tebas. Gulick, Lane and Masur each wrote “None.”[14, 17]Lane wrote “None” while serving as the last-named author of ACTT-1, the NIAID-sponsored trial whose results carried the panel’s remdesivir recommendation. The trial paper says Gilead employees took part in protocol discussions and weekly calls, and that NIAID “ultimately made all decisions.”[18] NIAID’s statisticians proposed changing the trial’s main measure to time to recovery on 22 March 2020, after about 7 percent of patients had enrolled; the amendment is dated 1 April. FDA’s reviewer called the change reasonable.[19] The Government Accountability Office found federal agencies spent about $162 million on remdesivir research through 2020 and ended up with no patent rights; Gilead held them.[20]
Eight weeks that decided the drugThe sequence is the story, so here it is in order.
18 March 2020. Fauci’s diary: HHS Secretary Alex Azar “said that he could approve HC and Remdesivir now with the powers that he has... I took a deep breath and said that this was wrong and should not be done.”[21]
21 April. The panel’s first guidelines find “insufficient clinical data to recommend either for or against” remdesivir.[14]
28 April. Gilead’s Merdad Parsey asks Fauci to hold the trial announcement “so that they can formulate a statement and policy to not allow an unfavorable or too favorable response of the Stock Market.” Fauci writes that he told him no way, and that Parsey backed off.[22]
29 April. NIAID announces the results. An email that morning says FDA “[has] written (and cleared with Gilead) a new sentence” for the NIH press release. Gilead’s own statement reached Fauci “before markets open this morning.”[23] At the White House that day Fauci says remdesivir “will be the standard of care,” in the same remarks calling the 31 percent improvement something that “doesn’t seem like a knock-out.”[24]
1 May. FDA issues the emergency authorization on “topline data,” with distribution “controlled by the United States (U.S.) Government.”[25] Gilead’s chief executive stands in the Oval Office with the President.[26]
12 May. The panel flips from “insufficient clinical data” to recommending remdesivir for severe disease, “on the basis of preliminary clinical trial data.” That is thirteen days after “standard of care.”[27]Five months later the largest remdesivir trial reported. WHO’s Solidarity study followed 11,330 hospitalized patients and found 301 deaths among 2,743 on remdesivir against 303 among 2,708 on standard care, with no reduction in ventilator use or hospital stay.[28] That was 15 October. FDA approved remdesivir a week later on the strength of NIAID’s trial; the review does not discuss Solidarity.[29, 30] On 2 November a Medicare payment that names remdesivir began paying.[7] On 20 November WHO’s guideline panel, reporting no conflict of interest among its members, conditionally recommended against remdesivir for hospitalized patients.[31] The NIH panel’s guideline cited Solidarity for the first time on 11 February 2021.[27]NIAID’s own trial found patients recovered in a median of 10 days on remdesivir against 15 on placebo. Deaths by day 29 were 11.4 percent against 15.2 percent, a difference too small to count statistically.[18] Solidarity, the French DisCoVeRy trial of 857 patients and the 2023 Cochrane review all found little or no effect on deaths in hospitalized patients.[28, 32, 33] Gilead’s Veklury sales were $2.8 billion in 2020, $5.6 billion in 2021 and $3.9 billion in 2022.[34, 35, 36]
The dealThe agreement that governed who got remdesivir from July through September 2020 is a three-party memorandum dated 27 June 2020, between HHS, Gilead and the drug distributor AmerisourceBergen. HHS did not buy the drug. Hospitals paid. HHS’s Assistant Secretary for Preparedness and Response, Robert Kadlec, signed for the government.[5]The terms read like a franchise agreement. Gilead would “use commercially reasonable efforts” to supply about 501,900 treatment courses for July through September. “ASPR will set allocation quantities,” and Gilead and the distributor “shall have no responsibility or discretion” over which hospitals got the drug. The price was $520 a vial, about $3,250 a course. If Gilead could not sell August or September allocated stock by 31 October, even after offering it to foreign governments, “HHS agrees to indemnify Gilead ... for the losses associated with the Excess Product at $390 per vial,” up to 145,000 courses, a ceiling of about $353 million. And the memorandum states that the PREP Act’s immunity and pre-emption protections “extend to the participation of Gilead and Distributor in this MOU.”[5]Under HHS’s plan the preparedness office set each state’s share and state health departments chose the hospitals.[37] New Jersey’s memo of 26 June 2020, written for the donated stock a day before the memorandum, shows how one state ran it: report twice a week, and “Failure to report data may negatively affect qualification for future allocations.” It left the prescribing call to “the attending physician of record.”[38]Seven weeks before Kadlec signed, six Democratic senators wrote that they were “concerned by recent reports” that he had “failed to disclose” to the Senate and the Office of Government Ethics that he co-founded a company in 2012 and consulted for Emergent BioSolutions, which had received more than $733 million from his office.[39] Emergent paid his consulting firm $120,000 a year from 2012 to 2015. Emergent’s executive chairman confirmed the $360,000 total under oath on 19 May 2021.[40] The stockpile moved from CDC to Kadlec’s office in 2018. The Washington Post reported that moving it was part of Emergent’s 2017 corporate strategy.[41, 39]On 11 February 2020, Fauci’s diary shows Kadlec offering Japan remdesivir under compassionate use for Diamond Princess passengers, before any trial had reported.[42] The memorandum wrote the Secretary’s PREP Act immunity into the deal.
The bonusSection 3710 of the CARES Act, signed 27 March 2020, orders Medicare to raise the payment weight of any hospital stay for “an individual diagnosed with COVID-19” by 20 percent.[6] That is the bonus the nurse described. It was 15 percent when it first appeared.On 19 March the Senate Republican leadership’s bill, S. 3548, carried a 15 percent add-on. The Finance Committee’s own summary of it says 15.[43, 44] The American Hospital Association told its members that same day to ask their lawmakers for “a Medicare add-on payment equal to 25% of the diagnosis-related group.”[45] On Friday 20 March the association’s advisory still described 15. By Sunday 22 March, as the Republicans released a revised bill, its advisory described 20.[46] A House Ways and Means summary dated 23 March, describing the Senate text as of Sunday 22 March, said the add-on “is more generous than earlier drafts: 20 percent, as compared to 15 percent in the first draft.”[47]Nobody has said who changed the number. The hospital lobbies were loud in those days. On 20 March the Federation of American Hospitals raised its funding request to $225 billion. On 21 March the association’s executive vice president told Modern Healthcare he expected the Senate’s opening offer to be “massaged and improved.”[48] Politico called the $100 billion hospital fund that followed “a major win for hospital lobbies” and wrote that “provider lobbyists in the past several days moved the needle considerably on funding talks.”[49] The Federation’s chief executive said of the finished bill: “It provides what we asked for.”[50]The second payment came in November. CMS’s rule for the new COVID-19 treatments add-on pays part of a stay’s extra cost on stays that used a listed product, a ceiling of roughly $19,500 a case at the rule’s own example threshold of about $30,000. The rule lists two products: convalescent plasma and remdesivir. CMS said the purpose was to avoid “financial disincentives for hospitals to provide new COVID-19 treatments.”[7, 51] Ivermectin and hydroxychloroquine were not on the list.The relief fund dwarfed both. HHS said in August 2021 it was “distributing $178 billion to hospitals and healthcare providers.” The Government Accountability Office found providers kept $135 billion, about $84 billion of it to hospital-based systems. The first $30 billion went out by each provider’s share of Medicare fee-for-service payments, not by COVID cases.[52, 53, 54]The $40,000 ventilator figure in the nurse’s post matches a Kaiser Family Foundation study of 2017 Medicare claims ($40,218) that excluded the 20 percent bonus; it is not a CMS estimate. The $24,000 figure matches no Medicare figure in that study.[55] The real average, from the HHS inspector general’s audit of $2.7 billion in COVID claims for September to November 2020, was about $16,300 a claim.[56] Nurses say they were told to code patients as COVID for the money. The inspector general audited that question on a sample of 149 of 166,107 claims and found 146 correct and three wrong. The sample covered three months of Medicare fee-for-service claims. The claims at the hospitals named in Johnson’s testimonies have not been pulled.
The lobby inside the billing systemThe American Hospital Association told its members to ask for the bonus, tracked it through its member advisories, and then went to CMS to defend it. On 6 April it asked CMS to extend the 20 percent to long-term care hospitals.[57] In August CMS announced that for admissions from 1 September it would require a positive COVID test on the record to keep the money, and said it would recoup the payment if none was there.[58] The association wrote to CMS Administrator Seema Verma on 26 August: “we urge CMS to allow provider documentation to suffice if the test result is unavailable.” Its reasoning: “The U07.1 diagnosis code therefore remains sufficient for identifying COVID-19 cases for the DRG add-on policy.”[59]The association does not only lobby the billing system. It chairs and staffs part of it. It owns the copyright on the UB-04 billing manual, which the National Uniform Billing Committee calls “the only official source of UB Data.” AHA staff chair that committee and hold its secretariat, and the committee told hospitals how to flag COVID claims on 23 March 2020, four days before the law was signed.[60] The association is one of four “Cooperating Parties” that approve the ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines, which federal law makes mandatory and which say, of COVID, that “the provider’s documentation that the individual has COVID-19 is sufficient” to assign the code the bonus is keyed to.[61, 62] The association spent $19.5 million lobbying in 2020, its own filings show.[63]The Federation of American Hospitals’ first-quarter filing says it “advocated in support of lifting sequester, increasing DRG payments.”[64]Now the file. The Senate Finance Committee’s own 19 March summary of the add-on carries the author tag “Baker, Brett (Finance).”[44] The Finance Republicans’ health staff in those years included a Brett Baker: Senior Advisor, Health Policy under Chuck Grassley in 2018, and Deputy Health Policy Director under Mike Crapo by February 2021.[65] In April 2022 a Brett Baker is a registered lobbyist for the American Hospital Association at The Nickles Group, the firm that was already the association’s outside lobbyist in 2020. His form lists Senate Finance Committee jobs under Crapo, Grassley and Hatch, “Deputy Health Policy Director; Health Policy Dir.; Senior Policy Advsr; Policy Advisor,” and a House Ways and Means professional-staff post as his government experience.[66] That is a revolving door: a senior Finance Republican health aide through February 2021 is the hospital lobby’s man in 2022.
What reached the bedsideJames Miller was a trauma and acute-care surgeon who also worked in critical care at Providence Regional Medical Center Everett in Washington State, the hospital that treated the first American COVID patient.[67] He signed a 72-paragraph declaration under penalty of perjury on 31 May 2024. It names the hospital officials who, he swears, carried the federal requirements to the staff.[12]In late February or early March 2020, he swears, Stephen Campbell, chief medical officer of the Providence Medical Group, informed him that “the CDC had sent us a powerful antiviral.” Miller says the drug was “understood to be remdesivir, which was given to the hospital as compassionate use directly from the CDC,” and swears Campbell’s representations about its effectiveness were “inaccurate.”[12] The New England Journal of Medicine’s report on the first U.S. case confirms that doctors at Providence “pursued compassionate use” of remdesivir for him.[67]
“The Chief Medical Officer, Jay Cook, would send out weekly to daily directives to the staff and physicians providing updates of the CDC and CMS requirements ... throughout the entire COVID crisis (over one year). ... it was understood that you would lose your job and/or license if you did not maintain compliance with the unscientific and constantly shifting federal health requirements.” Dr. James Miller, sworn declaration, 2024.[12]Miller swears that masking, ventilator use, protective equipment, staff vaccination, distancing and the shutdown of elective surgery “were all determined by the federal health agencies and forced upon the staff and patients by the hospital administrators.” He swears that after the directives began, “the hospital’s unanticipated mortality in indexed trauma surgery patients increased by more than 100% (doubled),” and that “the administration was confronted with this data and made no changes.”[12] He swears he found Medicare fraud by several providers in March 2020, “with the approval of the Chief Medical Officer of the hospital,” reported it to authorities, and that administrators then tried to fabricate grounds to fire him and go after his license. He swears the default on death certificates assigned to him was COVID, and that the hospital’s COVID numbers turned downward on or about 17 March 2020 while leadership went on publishing inflated counts and collecting federal aid.[12] After he resigned in January 2022, he swears, four requests for a fair hearing on a “microaggression” investigation that cleared him were denied by Cook, the chief of surgery and two committee https://t.co/UDonViyg1z Miller’s account those directives carried the CDC and CMS requirements to the hospital’s staff. No copy is public. Washington’s public records law covers state and local agencies, not a private hospital system like Providence, and state law shields hospital peer-review files.[68, 69, 70] The copies sit in Providence’s system and in the inboxes of the physicians who received them. A Senate committee’s letter to Providence is the tool that gets them.Other doctors fought the protocols at their own cost. Paul Marik, a critical-care physician in Norfolk, Virginia, sued Sentara Healthcare on 9 November 2021 over its ban on ivermectin and other drugs in his protocol. He swore that he believed about half the patients admitted to his ICU had received or were getting remdesivir, and that he does not prescribe it and stops it. The injunction hearing was on 18 November, the date on a letter suspending his privileges for 14 days that Marik found on 20 November. The judge denied the injunction on 23 November. Sentara’s own guidelines listed remdesivir starting criteria drawn from the NIAID trial and did not require the drug.[71]
What the evidence said, and what the protocols didEarly in 2020 the profession’s own guideline told doctors to watch patients on high-flow oxygen and “early intubation in a controlled setting if worsening occurs.”[72] Reported deaths among ventilated COVID patients averaged 45 percent across 69 studies and 57,420 patients.[73] At Northwell in New York, by 4 April 2020, 24.5 percent of 1,151 ventilated patients had died and 72.2 percent were still in hospital; the claim that 88 percent died divides 282 by the 320 whose outcome was known.[74]One steroid worked. Britain’s RECOVERY trial, funded in part by the Wellcome Trust and the Gates Foundation, showed dexamethasone helped patients on oxygen or ventilators, and NIH recommended it for ventilated patients and for patients on supplemental oxygen on 25 June 2020.[75, 76] The panel recommended against hydroxychloroquine in June 2020 and against ivermectin in August 2020 outside a trial. In February 2021 it moved ivermectin to “insufficient evidence ... to recommend either for or against.”[77, 78, 79] The payment rule named neither drug.
Visitors, mandates and the shieldOn 13 March 2020 CMS told nursing homes to “restrict visitation of all visitors and non-essential health care personnel, except for certain compassionate care situations, such as an end-of-life situation.” David R. Wright signed it.[8] CMS’s later visitation memo, QSO-20-39-NH, revised on 8 May 2023 as the emergency ended, says “Visitation is allowed for all residents at all times.”[80] The nurse’s post called the policy “the same green light to lock families out”; the first federal visitation memo was this one.[3]On 5 November 2021 CMS required 15 types of Medicare- and Medicaid-certified providers, hospitals and nursing homes among them, to ensure their staff were vaccinated. CMS Administrator Chiquita Brooks-LaSure approved the rule and HHS Secretary Xavier Becerra signed it.[9] Two federal courts blocked it in late November. On 13 January 2022 the Supreme Court stayed both injunctions, five to four, with Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch and Barrett dissenting.[81] CMS withdrew it in June 2023.[82]The legal shield is older than both. Azar signed the PREP Act declaration on 10 March 2020, putting into effect the Act’s rule that, “subject to other provisions,” a covered person “shall be immune from suit and liability under federal and state law with respect to all claims for loss caused by, arising out of, relating to, or resulting from the administration to or use by an individual of a covered countermeasure,” except for claims of “willful misconduct.”[10] HHS has amended it twelve times. The twelfth, signed by Becerra in December 2024, runs it to 31 December 2029.[11] Injured patients go to a federal compensation program; only willful-misconduct claims can reach court. As of 1 July 2026 it had received 14,146 COVID claims, decided 7,584, found 112 eligible and paid 62.[83]

I owe the oil business an apology.

I'm 58.  I spent 20 years in private equity.  Which means for 20 years I was the guy asking for the report.  The monthly one.  The quarterly one.  The one "real quick before the board meeting."  I never once wondered who built them.

Turns out it was somebody like her.

Somewhere in Midland tonight a reg tech is pulling numbers off the RRC site by hand.  Same as last month.  She's missing her kid's ballgame to do it.

That's a job for a gopher.

So I did what any guilty old man would do.  I built software to fix it.

Kidding.  Smarter people built it.  I'm the one they let talk.

RIGGS is an AI workspace built for oil and gas.  You spin up agents.  We call them gophers.  (You really didn't think we'd call them agents in the oilfield, did you?)  A gopher reads your well files, pulls from the RRC, the OCD, the OCC, writes the report, and does it again next month without anybody asking.

Your data is your data.  We don't train on it.

The offer: we sit down with your team.  You bring the job everybody dreads every week.  You build the gopher yourself before we leave the room.

DM me.  I can't give her the ballgames back.  I can get her to the next one.

In July 2024, Kang appeared at the groundbreaking of a second major project: a roughly $5 billion data-center development in Liangshan (凉山), a remote area of Sichuan province. Local official accounts identified him as chairman of a Century Longteng-affiliated data-services unit.

Corporate filings also link Century Longteng interests to yet another data-center development in Shenzhen.

As Kang built up a data-center business, Alice Huang was trying to set up a pipeline of Nvidia chips in 2023 and pursued a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang.

By Nov 2023, Megaspeed had told Nvidia that Alibaba would be an anchor customer, and earned a designation as an Nvidia cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips. 

That same month, Alice Huang’s registered directorship at Megaspeed ended amid an ownership restructuring, but the relationship with Jensen Huang continued. She and Jensen Huang were photographed together at a Singapore restaurant in late 2023 and again the following year at the Computex tech conference in Taipei.

The couple also pitched their ventures to outside investors. Between late 2024 and June 2025, they offered several data-center projects in Shanghai and Southeast Asia, telling potential investors they could expect to triple their money in three years.

They expressed confidence they had ways to bring Nvidia chips into China.

The couple’s activities soon drew scrutiny.

In Feb 2025, Singapore launched an investigation into Megaspeed and its key officers over suspected false declarations on server purchases. Authorities ultimately found insufficient evidence of domestic criminal offenses but issued Alice Huang a stern warning and barred her from re-entering Singapore. Investigations into Megaspeed and six other individuals remain ongoing.

Kang had been detained in Shanghai earlier this year in connection with stock-market manipulation inquiries. He has recently been released and shared a photo of himself at Stanford University with friends.

text:
Compared to a company like SpaceX, things still operate quite a bit differently.

When balancing cost, time, and scope, the cost is considered fixed. It is preplanned both annually and quarterly ahead of time, is very rigid and not really open to change. No work can begin on a project without funding secured for it first.

If deadlines were approaching, or got hit, we would either delay the release and/or cut scope long before we ever required anyone to work overtime to make up for it. Work-life balance was very important.

SpaceX works their engineers very hard with tons of crunch time and require them to live and work in pretty undesirable locations. Traditionally defense companies are generally located in red state metros in fairly desirable family-friendly areas. We have much less turnover as a result.

No RSUs were ever offered of course.

One of the biggest inhibitors to innovation at traditional aerospace & defense companies is that people like to establish their own little fiefdoms and don’t let others step on their toes if they think they have a better idea. It is very difficult for one engineer to escalate and overrule another engineer or manager that they feel is the wrong approach. People are very protective of their little fiefdoms and don’t like outside interference.

A big reason I started my own projects is because I saw incompetence in the technical direction being pursued on the safety-critical graphics team for my last employer. The technical leadership on the team had no interest in improving determinism at lower cost, dismissing it out of hand. I did have a Senior Tech Fellow as a mentor who had my back but he like many others lacked any authority to enact change.

text:
A lot of people have real trouble thinking about the aggregate behavior of groups. They can only think about individuals. 

So they think about Elon Musk as an individual. Maybe they think that he must be retarded, because they need that for emotional reasons. Or maybe they think he is a talented rocket designer. 

But even if they realize he understands rockets, they can only think about him as an individual doing tasks. Not about his impact on what the whole company does. 

If Elon Musk is just a talented rocket designer, then he can spend all day, every day, improving rocket designs. 

But he is just one of 7000 engineers. So even if did a perfect job, he would only improve progress by about .014% 

So, when a midwit looks at SpaceX, he sees 7000 engineers, and says to himself "Elon Musk cannot possibly be designing the whole damn rocket himself. These people are giving him too much credit."

This would be absolutely true if Musk were just a some random SpaceX engineer. But he isn't. He's the absolute dictator of the whole damn company. 

He decides, with absolute and unquestionable authority, which behaviors are punished and which are rewarded. 

Why is this important? 

When I worked at Boeing, on various classified projects, I naively came in with the assumption that I was a software engineer, employed to design and build functional software as quickly and cheaply as possible. 

Because of this, I focused on functionality and efficiency, for example suggesting changes that would obviate the need for entire projects and software components. 

And I very rapidly became persona non grata. 

At first, this caused me to adopt an air of aggrieved innocence. I was just trying to do my job well, and I was being punished for it. 

Then I gradually came to realize that I hadn't properly understood what my job was, or what the actual mission of Boeing Defense, Space, and Security was. 

Boeing DSS was not an aerospace company. Boeing DSS was a fraud company. 

Its goal was twofold. First, to maximize transfer of public tax dollars to stockholder pockets. Second, to maintain the appearance of being an aerospace company, to prevent the fraud from being exposed. 

Which meant that my real job was twofold. First, to generate billable hours. Second, to look busy. 

This is why Space Launch System sucks. Why it is always late when it doesn't fail outright. Why it is at 300% of its target budget. Why it leaves American astronauts stranded and needing a lift from SpaceX. 

That's because, for Boeing, building rockets is a side quest. Something they have to do to look busy. Yes, a rocket does occasionally fly, but that's just happening so programs don't get shut down. 

For Boeing, coming in early and under budget would actually be failure. The system is functioning exactly as designed. 

The cost, not the rocket, is the goal. 

Musk and SpaceX don't work like that. 

Unlike Boeing executives, Musk is not a useless grifter asshole. He is an entirely different kind of asshole... a rocket obsessed sperg. 

So, at SpaceX, engineers do not get rewarded for generating billable hours. They get rewarded for making rockets fly. And for all the subtasks of this, like figuring out how to make rockets lighter, figuring out how to make engines reignite better, figuring out how to make rocket exhaust not destroy launch pads, etc. 

And this attracts engineers who care about rockets. You've seen them on broadcasts, crying on open microphones because they dedicated their lives to something and it just flew. 

As a rocket engineer, who designs rockets, Musk is probably replaceable. As a rocket company engineer, who designs rocket companies, he is not. 

For over 50 years, the US space industry stagnated precisely for the lack of a Musk-like figure, who could not only create an effective aerospace company, but who could thereby demonstrate what an effective aerospace company looks like. 

Which makes it much more difficult for fraudsters to get away with fraud. 

I'm envious. I wish I could have worked for an aerospace company instead of a fraud company. 

But what's more important is that some of us now no longer have to play "who gets the most cheese?". 

They get to play "What can we build today?".

DraftKings sued for using AI to find gamblers most likely to keep losing money

DraftKings is facing a proposed federal class-action lawsuit filed in October 2026 in the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts by plaintiff Daniel Vest.

Key Details of the Lawsuit and Investigations
🔹 The Allegations: The suit and a related New York Times investigation charge that DraftKings used an artificial intelligence and machine-learning model (reportedly nicknamed "the score") to analyze customer betting habits, account balances, and loss-to-bet ratios.
🔹 Targeting Losing Bettors: The model allegedly identified gamblers who were most likely to continue losing money and re-engaged them with heavy promotional offers, profit boosts, emails, and dozens of push notifications to induce more wagers.
🔹 Suppressed Responsible Gaming Tools: Former employees alleged that while the profit-driven AI model was actively refined and deployed, internal efforts to use similar predictive tech to flag and protect problem gamblers were stalled or shelved because high-losing or "elastic" bettors make up a massive share of platform revenue.
🔹 Relief Sought: The lawsuit demands a jury trial, financial damages, refunds, disgorgement, and injunctive relief, claiming DraftKings breached implied contracts and state regulations. [1]
🔹 DraftKings' Response: DraftKings has strongly denied the accusations, stating that its promotions are aimed at users with sustained engagement rather than targeting people based on losses or problem gambling indicators, and has vowed to vigorously fight the litigation.
🔹 Regulatory Scrutiny: Beyond the lawsuit, the Massachusetts Gaming Commission launched an inquiry into the company's AI practices, and state and federal lawmakers (including scrutiny in states like Louisiana and New York) have ramped up reviews of automated personalized gambling promotions.

text:
Commonwealth v. Aidan Kearney

This time, Special Assistant District Attorney Robert C. Cosgrove is asking Judge Belezos to restrict defense opening statements to what prosecutors consider the proper legal boundaries AND require advance identification of any visual aids, exhibits, or demonstrative materials the defense intends to show jurors.

The prosecution also wants an opportunity to challenge those materials before the jury sees them.

Here's what the filing actually says.

🔶 1. THE COMMONWEALTH WANTS LIMITATIONS ON THE DEFENSE'S OPENING STATEMENT.

Prosecutors are asking Judge Belezos to instruct Kearney's defense attorneys to comply with Rule 24 of the Massachusetts Rules of Criminal Procedure.

The Commonwealth argues that opening statements should be limited to outlining evidence counsel reasonably expects to present during trial.

According to the motion, opening statements are intended to help jurors understand the evidence they will hear, not serve as an opportunity for attorneys to argue their case.

The Commonwealth also emphasizes that attorneys should not make statements they cannot support with evidence.

🔶 2. THE PROSECUTION RAISES THE POSSIBILITY OF PROFESSIONAL MISCONDUCT.

This part caught my attention.

The Commonwealth quotes the reporter's note to Rule 24, which warns that making unsupported statements concerning significant elements of a case can constitute professional misconduct.

The filing also argues that allowing an attorney to make unsupported assertions intended to influence the jury would be fundamentally unfair to the opposing party.

To be clear, the motion does NOT identify a specific statement that Aidan's defense attorneys have made or intend to make.

It is asking for a prospective ruling governing their opening statements.

🔶 3. THE COMMONWEALTH WANTS TO KNOW WHAT VISUAL AIDS THE DEFENSE PLANS TO USE.

The prosecution is requesting an order requiring the defense to identify in advance any:

▪️ Visual aids.

▪️ Potential exhibits.

▪️ Demonstrative materials, sometimes called "chalks."

▪️ Other materials intended to be displayed during opening statements.

That means prosecutors want advance notice of the materials the defense plans to put in front of the jury before the first witness even testifies.

🔶 4. THE COMMONWEALTH WANTS A CHANCE TO OBJECT BEFORE THE JURY SEES THOSE MATERIALS.

The motion explains that, during opening statements, evidence generally has not yet been formally admitted.

Prosecutors argue that without advance notice, they would not have an opportunity to object before the defense displays a proposed exhibit or visual aid.

The Commonwealth therefore requests a ruling on the admissibility of any proposed evidence.

This is an important distinction:

The prosecution is not simply asking the defense to identify its visual materials.

It is also asking the court to address potential admissibility objections before those materials are displayed.

🔶 5. THE COMMONWEALTH OFFERS AN ALTERNATIVE REQUEST.

If Judge Belezos does not require advance identification and rulings, prosecutors ask that the defense be required to submit copies of everything displayed to the jury during opening statements.

Those materials would then be marked for identification, creating a record of what jurors were shown.

That alternative would document the defense's presentation rather than necessarily requiring advance approval of every visual aid.

🔶 6. NOW COMPARE MOTION #8 WITH MOTION #6.

This is where things get interesting.

In Motion #6, the Commonwealth requested permission to use computer-assisted technology to display exhibits, diagrams, demonstrative evidence, and excerpts from lengthy video recordings.

Now, in Motion #8, the Commonwealth wants the defense to identify its proposed opening-statement visuals in advance and give prosecutors an opportunity to object.

These are not identical requests. Motion #6 concerns the prosecution's presentation of evidence more broadly, while Motion #8 specifically addresses defense opening statements.

But the comparison raises a fair question:

Will the court apply comparable standards of accuracy, fairness, disclosure, and admissibility to visual presentations offered by BOTH sides?

Because the rules should protect the integrity of the proceedings regardless of which party is presenting the material.

🔶 7. Here is a recap of the requests we've reviewed:

🟠 Motion #1: Restrict references to alleged bad character or prior misconduct of victims and witnesses.

🟠 Motion #2: Require advance notice and preliminary rulings concerning defense questioning about witness bias.

🟠 Motion #3: Require preliminary questioning of proposed character and reputation witnesses.

🟠 Motion #4: Admit Kearney's out-of-court statements, including recorded statements.

🟠 Motion #5: Impound juror names and sidebar discussions until a verdict.

🟠 Motion #6: Permit the Commonwealth to use visual presentations, diagrams, and excerpts from lengthy recordings.

🟠 Motion #7: Sequester witnesses during trial.

🟠 Motion #8: Restrict defense opening statements to proper evidentiary subjects and require advance identification or documentation of defense visual aids.

EIGHT MOTIONS, WITH SEVERAL SEEKING PRETRIAL CONTROL OVER HOW THE DEFENSE MAY QUESTION WITNESSES OR PRESENT ITS CASE.

Some of these requests involve standard courtroom procedures.

But the cumulative effect of any restrictions will depend on how broadly Judge Belezos interprets and applies them.

🔶 HERE ARE MY QUESTIONS:

▪️ What specific defense visuals is the Commonwealth concerned about?

▪️ Does the prosecution anticipate that the defense will present materials challenging the investigation or witness credibility?

▪️ Will similar advance-review requirements apply to prosecution opening-statement visuals?

▪️ Could advance review prevent unfair surprise without unnecessarily restricting the defense?

HERE IS WHAT I KEEP COMING BACK TO.

A criminal defendant has the right to present a defense, challenge the prosecution's evidence, and receive a fair trial.

That does not mean defense attorneys can introduce inadmissible evidence or make unsupported claims during opening statements.

But it does mean that any restrictions should be legally justified and applied fairly.

I want to see how Kearney's attorneys, Timothy Bradl and Mark Bederow, respond to these requests.

A fair trial isn't about giving either side an advantage. It's about allowing the jury to hear legally admissible evidence and reach its own verdict.

The Commonwealth has requested these restrictions. The filing does not establish that Judge Belezos has granted them.

Aidan Kearney remains presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

text:
Commonwealth v. Aidan Kearney

This is the THIRD motion addressing potential testimony about witnesses, their credibility, character, or alleged bias.

Special Assistant District Attorney Robert C. Cosgrove is now asking Judge Belezos to require the defense to identify witnesses who may offer opinions about the character or reputation of Aidan Kearney or any other witness.

And the prosecution wants those witnesses questioned by the court BEFORE the jury is allowed to hear their testimony.

Here's what the filing says.

🔶 1. THE COMMONWEALTH WANTS THE DEFENSE TO IDENTIFY CHARACTER AND REPUTATION WITNESSES.

Prosecutors are asking the court to require the defense to identify anyone expected to offer testimony concerning:

🔸 Aidan Kearney's character or reputation.

🔸 The character or reputation of any witness.

🔸 Opinions concerning those individuals.

The Commonwealth wants to know who may provide this testimony before it is presented to jurors.

🔶 2. PROSECUTORS WANT A VOIR DIRE HEARING BEFORE THE JURY HEARS THE TESTIMONY.

The motion asks Judge Belezos to conduct voir dire of these witnesses.

In this context, voir dire means preliminary questioning to determine whether a witness has a legally sufficient foundation to offer the proposed testimony.

The prosecution wants the judge to establish whether that foundation exists before allowing the jury to hear the testimony.

🔶 3. THE COMMONWEALTH CLAIMS IT COULD BE SERIOUSLY PREJUDICED.

The motion states:

“The Commonwealth would be seriously prejudiced by an inadmissible, although inadvertent, answer to foundation and general reputation questions.”

Essentially, prosecutors argue that even an unintended inadmissible answer could improperly influence the jury.

They maintain that questioning witnesses outside the jury's presence would prevent that possibility.

🔶 4. THE PROSECUTION CITES MASSACHUSETTS CASE LAW ABOUT WITNESS CREDIBILITY.

The Commonwealth relies on Commonwealth v. Dockham and Commonwealth v. Walker.

The motion quotes legal authority recognizing that a witness may testify about another witness's general reputation for truthfulness among people who know that individual.

However, it also argues that testimony about specific acts of lying or similar misconduct, or personal opinions about the character of a witness being impeached, is not admissible under the cited rule.

There is an important distinction between testimony about someone's general reputation for truthfulness and testimony about particular alleged incidents of dishonesty.

🔶 5. THIS IS NOW THE THIRD MOTION CONCERNING HOW THE DEFENSE MAY CHALLENGE WITNESSES.

Look at what the Commonwealth has requested so far:

🟠 Motion #1: Exclude references to alleged bad character or prior misconduct involving alleged victims or witnesses.

🟠 Motion #2: Require advance notice and a preliminary ruling before the defense questions witnesses about alleged bias or prejudice.

🟠 Motion #3: Require the defense to identify proposed character or reputation witnesses and have them questioned outside the jury's presence before their testimony is admitted.

THREE MOTIONS. THREE DIFFERENT REQUESTS CONCERNING WHAT THE DEFENSE MAY PRESENT TO THE JURY.

Now, motions in limine are a normal part of trial preparation, and prosecutors are entitled to seek rulings on potentially inadmissible evidence.

But that doesn't mean these requests should escape scrutiny.

HERE IS WHAT I WANT TO KNOW:

🔸 Which witnesses does the Commonwealth anticipate the defense may call to challenge someone's reputation for truthfulness?

🔸 What testimony is the prosecution concerned the jury might hear?

🔸 Will the defense argue that the requested procedures are unnecessary or overly restrictive?

🔸 How will Judge Belezos balance the rules of evidence against Kearney's right to present a defense and challenge the credibility of witnesses testifying against him?

LET'S NOT FORGET SOMETHING IMPORTANT.

When the credibility of witnesses matters to a criminal prosecution, the defense must have a meaningful opportunity to challenge that credibility through legally admissible evidence.

The jury is responsible for evaluating the witnesses and determining what testimony it believes.

The court's responsibility is to ensure that the evidence presented complies with the law while protecting the defendant's constitutional rights.

The Commonwealth has now filed three motions seeking advance restrictions or procedures governing defense evidence about witnesses.

text:
Somewhere in your firm there's a data strategy deck with a lake on page three. Somewhere else, a dozen people are running their own AI experiments. Neither effort has reached the place where an advisor prepares for a client review, and the people funding both are starting to ask why. The two efforts rest on opposite myths, and both fail for the same reason.

The first myth says the key first step is a data strategy that gets all of the company's data into a lake, warehouse, or lakehouse so AI has context. It has serious backing. McKinsey, the consulting firm, wrote on Sept. 15, 2023: "If your data isn't ready for generative AI, your business isn't ready for generative AI." Gartner, the research firm, predicted on Feb. 26, 2025 that through 2026 organizations "will abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data." Piyush Gupta, chief executive of Singapore's DBS Bank, told McKinsey on Feb. 10, 2025: "You have to be thoughtful about how you create and architect your data lakes." He said the cleanup and migration took "more than ten years and about a 100-person data factory." He also described building demonstrable use cases along the way to show value.

The second myth says to let every employee build their own small AI prototypes and expect them to add up to an enterprise capability. The results so far say otherwise. MIT's NANDA initiative, a research group at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, studied this in its July 2025 report "The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025." It found 95 percent of organizations getting no measurable P&L return from generative AI. For custom or vendor-sold enterprise tools, 60 percent of organizations evaluated them, 20 percent reached pilot, and 5 percent reached production. The authors did not blame the models. They pointed to brittle workflows, a lack of contextual learning, and poor fit with day-to-day operations.

Data quality matters, and experiments have value. What fails is the sequence and the expectation of scale.

Gartner's 2024 roadmap "AI-Ready Data Essentials" says AI-ready data "must be representative of the use case." It adds that this readiness "is not something you can build once and for all, nor that you can build ahead of time for all your data." The first stage is to assess data needs depending on the AI use cases.

The record on big, ahead-of-time data programs is worse than the pitch. Gartner warned on July 28, 2014, in "Beware of the Data Lake Fallacy," that without descriptive metadata and a way to maintain it, "the data lake risks turning into a data swamp." Qlik, a data analytics vendor, quoted a Sept. 26, 2017 Gartner note in a press release: "Through 2018, 90 percent of deployed data lakes will be rendered useless, as they're overwhelmed with information assets captured for uncertain use cases." That was a prediction, not a measured failure rate, but the diagnosis is specific: data captured for uncertain use cases. McKinsey reported on Aug. 1, 2018 that one industrial company invested $15 million in big data infrastructure and did not start to see a payoff for at least three years. On Feb. 28, 2025, McKinsey wrote that most banks made significant data-transformation investments "in the past five to ten years," and that "most banks either could not finalize them or could not realize their expected impact." Unfinished programs left fragmented warehouses and lakes and "elevated costs from maintaining multiple complex environments."

McKinsey's March 4, 2024 guidance on generative AI names the alternative. Companies that do this well "tie their data quality and augmentation efforts to the specific AI/gen AI application and use case." In the same piece it says "you don't need this data foundation to extend to every corner of the enterprise."

A pilot proves that something can work for one person on one afternoon. A workflow has to work for a team, every week, with the same inputs and the same checks. The experiments are everywhere. Microsoft and LinkedIn's Work Trend Index, a May 2024 survey of 31,000 knowledge workers in 31 countries, found that 75 percent use generative AI at work, and 78 percent of those users bring their own AI tools. Salesforce, the enterprise software company, found in a November 2023 survey of more than 14,000 workers that more than half of generative AI users at work had no formal employer approval, and nearly 7 in 10 had never received training. Activity that wide, with no shared workflow behind it, rarely turns into production systems.

IDC, the market research firm, in research commissioned by Lenovo, the computer maker, and reported by the trade publication https://t.co/CXnu4U3b2K on March 25, 2025, found that for every 33 AI proofs of concept a company launched, only four reached production. IDC's authors blamed low readiness in data, processes, and IT. Ashish Nadkarni, a group vice president at IDC, said many proofs of concept are "born at the board level" and are "highly underfunded or not funded at all." Brian Jackson, a principal research director at Info-Tech Research Group, an IT research firm, offered the fair counterpoint: "even the failures are not failures if there are good lessons learned."

McKinsey's AI survey, fielded in July 2024 among 1,491 respondents and published March 12, 2025, found more than 80 percent not seeing a tangible impact on enterprise-level earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) from generative AI. Only 21 percent of those reporting gen AI use had "fundamentally redesigned at least some workflows." Of 25 attributes McKinsey tested, workflow redesign had the largest effect on EBIT impact. Its State of AI survey of 1,993 respondents, fielded from June 25 through July 29, 2025 and published Nov. 5, 2025, found 88 percent using AI in at least one function, yet nearly two-thirds had not begun scaling it across the enterprise. The same survey found use-case-level cost and revenue benefits, and 64 percent of respondents said AI was enabling innovation.

What gets AI into production is a short sequence. Start with one use case that has an owner and a place in someone's week. Pick the workflow it lives in, such as preparing for a client review or drafting the follow-up after one. List the data that job needs, and find where that data already lives. Fix the quality of that data for that job, and no more. Then build the AI step into the workflow, so the person doing the work meets it in the tool they already use.

The connection step used to be the hard part. Model Context Protocol, or MCP, is an open way for AI tools to connect to the systems where data already lives, so teams don't have to move everything into one lake first. Amazon Web Services, the cloud arm of Amazon, described the pattern in a Sept. 4, 2026 post on its Big Data Blog: instead of moving all data to one place, "let AI agents talk directly to the systems where data lives. Model Context Protocol (MCP) makes this possible." A lake can still earn its place. Ernst & Young (EY), the professional services firm, wrote in its 2026 paper "Model context protocols vs. enterprise data platforms": "The EDP governs the data; MCP governs the AI's access to that data."

Each use case that ships this way leaves behind cleaner data, a working connection, and a team that has seen the result. The next use case starts from there. Scale happens one workflow after another. It does not require a decade of preparation, and it does not come from a hundred scattered experiments that never meet.

Athena works with very large institutions and smaller RIAs. It's the AI-native platform built for how advisors work, and our MCP connection is live. We also help firms with their AI implementation.

If you want agitators to go away, just welcome them in. Extend your hand. They will never, ever square up with you intellectually. 

And who knows - maybe they know something you don’t. Maybe they’ll teach you something. If you’re willing to have the dialogue, at least you were open to the possibility. 

I’ve employed this with every political dispute ever. Every detractor, every malcontent, every critic —- every single one of them will never get on camera with you and levy their accusations in a place where you can respond and hold them accountable. Their entire facade would fall apart, and they don’t have the strength of their conviction. 

If you’re not willing to have your accusation be scrutinized, then you’re likely not serious or sober in your opinions. At the very least, you’re not genuine in your intent. 

It’s easy to lob ad hominem attacks. It takes intelligence and character to have your arguments withstand scrutiny. 

Never engage people anonymously. Be open to engaging real people wanting to hear your argument - even if they aren’t in your camp. Those are exactly the people you want to engage. 

People come to council meetings and sometimes shadow-box during comment sessions making crazy statements. The moment I offer to meet them privately and allow them to livestream it to the internet, they miraculously evaporate. 

It happens literally every single time.  

They just like the bully pulpit - they want to take swings, but never functionally dispute the issue at hand.

Their goal isn’t to understand, their goal is to hurt you. 

Recognize it and act accordingly.

text:
It was about 40 minutes into a midnight shift in April 2022, on a dark road along a reservoir in lower Fairfield County, Connecticut. Then a light filled Officer Robert Klein’s cruiser.  It was bright enough to blind him, and he could barely drive. 

Klein has 25 years in law enforcement. He told NewsNation’s Ashleigh Banfield what he saw when he stopped and looked up. It was a perfect sphere, roughly the size of a Mini Cooper, hovering about 30 feet from his patrol car.

It cycled through red, green, white and orange. He called it “plasma-like,” and he heard a low hum. He has seen plenty of drones and meteors on the job. He said this was nothing like them.

Klein aimed his spotlight at it. The object was instantly on the other side of the water. He could not follow its path from one point to the other. Only then did he snap out of it, grab his camera and start recording.

Klein told only a few colleagues. The first outside expert he contacted was Ben Hansen, a former FBI agent and host of UFO Witness on Discovery+.

His story finally aired in November 2024.

A researcher on Hansen’s team later posted that Klein’s dashcam was not running. It only records when his emergency lights are on. The same researcher says Klein’s fellow officers and his chief vouch for him.

Then a second witness came forward. Her name is Diane. She was on the back deck of a community center in Fairfield County when lights began moving across the sky. Hansen describes her report as two or three large orbs darting around and passing right over her head.

She is a skywatcher, and her first thought was a plane. The way the lights moved ruled that out for her.

Hansen says he checked the air traffic data and agrees it was not a plane. He also says several more witnesses have come forward. It may not be the first time. In late 2013, local writer Chris Burns documented an orange orb over the Saugatuck Reservoir. It appeared on three separate dates and hovered for 5 to 30 minutes each time. Online researchers believe the Saugatuck is the reservoir Klein was patrolling.

Here is where it gets messy. The skeptics at Metabunk went to work on Klein’s video. The file’s metadata says it was recorded at 11:22 p.m. on April 27, 2022. By matching tree lines in the frame to Street View images, they estimate the camera faced east-southeast, toward the south end of the reservoir.

Their claim is that at that moment, on that bearing, JetBlue Flight 1168 was in the line of sight. It was an Airbus A320.

Case closed? Not quite.

Another forum member filmed the same area and could not get the trees to line up. The animator who worked with Klein on NewsNation’s reenactment says the encounter is more complex than an oncoming plane. The forum never reached agreement.

Two different questions

This is the part most coverage misses.

Klein started recording after the object had already jumped across the water. That makes the video and the encounter two separate pieces of evidence.

If the light in the video is a JetBlue jet, that explains the video. It does not explain a color-shifting sphere 30 feet from a cruiser, bright enough to blind the officer inside.

Skeptics have offered ideas for that part too. One is an afterimage from looking into a bright light, which can seem to jump when your eyes move. No one has tested those ideas against Klein’s full account.

Your turn

Was it a plane, a trick of perception, or something that keeps coming back to the same reservoir?

If you live near the Saugatuck Reservoir or have seen lights there, tell me what you saw.

Sources: NewsNation, Metabunk

text:
LETTERS FROM STOCKHOLM
WIKE MUST GO: NIGERIA’S CAPITAL IS NOT A FAMILY INHERITANCE
By Kio Amachree

President Bola Tinubu should remove Nyesom Wike as Minister of the Federal Capital Territory and allow an independent investigation into the serious allegations surrounding his administration of Abuja’s land and his family’s reported assets.

A minister entrusted with the nation’s capital must answer questions about public property with documents, verifiable explanations and transparent accounts. Political usefulness cannot substitute for public accountability.

The published allegations involving Wike, his wife, his children, his father and other relatives demand precisely that scrutiny. They concern whether public authority has been used to build private family wealth. These allegations require investigation; they cannot responsibly be treated as convictions. Equally, Nigerians should not be expected to dismiss them because the official concerned is powerful.

The Abuja land allegations

In June 2025, Peoples Gazette alleged that approximately 2,082 hectares across the FCT had been allocated to Joaq Farms and Estates Limited, which it linked to Wike’s son Joaquin. The publication put their potential value at $3.6 billion, citing officials and allocation records. These are the newspaper’s allegations and estimates, not independently established losses to the treasury. 

A subsequent investigation alleged that 1,740 hectares, estimated at $2.85 billion, had been allocated to Jordan Farms and Estates and associated entities linked by the newspaper to Wike’s eldest son, Jordan. It also alleged that land previously allocated to the Austrian mission had been redirected through a company it associated with the family. 

Wike’s spokesman, Lere Olayinka, denied that any land had been allocated to the minister’s children. He acknowledged an agricultural allocation to JOAQ Farms in Bwari. In responding to the Jordan allegations, he maintained that Jordan Farms was a registered company whose directors did not include Wike’s children, and that a shared name did not establish ownership. 

Then publish the complete ownership records.

Publish the applications, allocation dates, assessments, payments and beneficial owners. Explain how the beneficiaries were selected and whether comparable applicants received comparable treatment.

A denial should begin the examination of the records. It should never end it.

The father, siblings and wider family

Reporting originating with Peoples Gazette alleged that Wike approved 33 land allocations to relatives and associates on 16 July 2025. Among the reported beneficiaries was his father, Joshua Nlemanya Wike, allegedly allocated 1,042 square metres in Guzape II, estimated by the reporting at approximately ₦400 million. 

The same reporting identified cousins and nephews, including Believe, Victor, Henry and Primise Wike. It also described earlier allocations to six people identified as his siblings, including Vincent Ejike Wike, Chidi Sam Wike and Chituru Wike. These remain reported allegations requiring examination of the original files. 

Relatives of a minister have the same right as other Nigerians to acquire property lawfully. The question is whether they received privileged access, preferential terms, waived obligations or benefits arising from their relationship with the person exercising public power.

Abuja belongs to Nigerians. No minister is entitled to administer it as a family estate.

The Florida properties and his wife’s reported role

In September 2025, Peoples Gazette reported that Justice Eberechi Suzzette Nyesom-Wike executed deeds transferring interests in three Florida homes to the couple’s children: Jordan, Joaquin and Jazmyne. The report described transfers in 2021 and 2023 and alleged that the properties had not been properly declared. It said neither Wike nor his wife provided substantive responses to its requests for comment. 

The publication alleged illicit funding, but that allegation requires a financial investigation. Property ownership, a purchase without mortgage financing and a transfer to children do not themselves establish money laundering.

The questions nevertheless deserve direct answers: who originally financed these homes, through which accounts, from what income, and what disclosures were required and made?

A judge’s involvement makes careful, independent scrutiny especially important. Judicial standing should strengthen the expectation of transparency.

Jordan Wike and the disputed $2.1 million

A separate controversy has reached an FCT High Court. Safwan Garba and his company allege that Jordan Wike received $2.1 million in connection with a failed Abuja property transaction. Jordan denies receiving the money or entering the transaction and says a signature attributed to him was forged. He produced his American passport in support of his account that he was outside Nigeria on the alleged payment date. The reporting reviewed does not establish a judgment finding him or his father liable. 

Arise News also reported an EFCC petition in which the complainants alleged that Jordan invoked his father’s approval and sought money purportedly intended to facilitate allocations. Those are the complainants’ accusations, not established facts. 

Investigators must establish what happened. The public deserves certainty about whether access to the minister’s office was offered, misrepresented or used in a private transaction.

Public money and the appearance of influence

The scrutiny extends beyond family assets.

Premium Times reported a ₦10 billion budget provision for rent and furniture for National Assembly presiding officers, alongside an increase in the allocation for judges’ housing to ₦30 billion. These spending provisions raise questions about priorities and institutional independence; they do not by themselves prove personal enrichment. 

SERAP challenged executive provision of houses and cars to judges. Wike defended the housing programme as an approved presidential welfare policy, rejecting suggestions that it was intended to compromise judges. 

An independent judiciary must be protected from both improper influence and the reasonable appearance of dependence on politically powerful benefactors.

Then there is the ₦39 billion International Conference Centre renovation. Wike defended the expenditure as a comprehensive refurbishment. Nigerians are entitled to demand the procurement records, detailed costs and an independent value-for-money assessment. An expensive project is not automatic evidence of theft, but public expenditure must withstand examination. 

The older electoral-bribery allegations

In 2017, a police panel alleged that officials received ₦360 million connected with the December 2016 Rivers legislative rerun elections and reported recovering ₦111 million. The Rivers government rejected the allegations as an attempt to implicate Wike and demanded proof. Charges against 23 INEC officials subsequently featured the alleged payments. Those reports do not establish a bribery conviction against Wike. 

Such matters deserve publicly traceable outcomes. Nigerians should be able to learn how serious allegations were resolved.

Remove him and open the records

This demand for scrutiny extends well beyond one commentator. A coalition reported as comprising 52 civil society organisations, including CISLAC and the Centre for Democracy and Development, called for investigations into alleged asset concealment and illicit enrichment involving Wike. 

President Tinubu should remove him from the ministry and permit institutions to work without political interference.

The EFCC, ICPC and Code of Conduct Bureau should independently examine the relevant transactions and disclosures. Any question involving judicial conduct should reach the appropriate judicial authorities. Investigators should preserve allocation files, establish beneficial ownership, trace purchase funds and publish their findings.

Where allegations fail, say so clearly. Where evidence establishes wrongdoing, prosecute the responsible individuals and recover assets through lawful proceedings.

Removal from ministerial office is a demand for political accountability. Criminal guilt must be established through evidence and due process.

Nigeria cannot build public confidence while serious allegations about public assets remain buried beneath political loyalty.

Mr President, open the records. Let investigators follow the money.

Wike must go. Abuja is the nation’s capital, not a family inheritance.

#LettersFromStockholm #TheKioSolution #Wike #PublicAccountability #AbujaLand #Nigeria

🚨 Breaking: ELON MUSK FIRES BACK AT JEFF BEZOS WITH A STRONG MESSAGE OVER TESLA’S POTENTIAL MOVE TO FLORIDA!

Elon Musk has reportedly delivered a blunt response to Jeff Bezos following his continued remarks about Tesla’s possible relocation of some of its operations to Florida.

Musk appears increasingly frustrated with Bezos weighing in on decisions concerning Tesla, making it clear that the company’s future is not something he intends to negotiate with another billionaire.

🗣️ ELON MUSK SAID:

“Jeff, I think it is time you focused on your own business and stopped concerning yourself with mine. Tesla is my responsibility, and every major decision we make will be based on what we believe is best for the company, our employees and our shareholders.

I don’t need permission from anyone to decide where Tesla should invest, expand or operate. I have spent years building this company, overcoming challenges and taking risks that many people thought were impossible. I will not allow outside commentary to dictate our next move.

If Florida offers better opportunities for Tesla’s future, we have every right to explore that possibility. That’s how business works. Companies make decisions based on growth, investment and long-term strategy, not on the opinions of competing billionaires.

You have Blue Origin and your own business ambitions to focus on. I have Tesla, SpaceX and my own responsibilities. We should both understand that distinction.

Competition is healthy, but constantly inserting yourself into another company’s decisions is unnecessary. I respect your right to have an opinion, but I also expect you to respect the boundaries of my business.

Let’s keep our attention on what we are each building. I have my own plans, and I intend to pursue them without unnecessary distractions.”

Musk’s message sends a clear signal: Tesla’s future will be determined by its own leadership, not by outside pressure or commentary from fellow billionaires.

To customers experiencing difficulties accessing their money at Chase, Wells Fargo or Bank of America, I understand your concerns. Banks and regulators must communicate openly, resolve service interruptions and provide customers with clear answers.

To passengers facing delays and cancellations, families waiting for loved ones, businesses struggling with interrupted transactions and workers unable to access essential communication services, I recognise the impact these disruptions are having on everyday life. People deserve dependable services and institutions that take their responsibilities seriously.

My administration will seek answers about what happened, demand accountability where appropriate and work with the relevant institutions to strengthen the systems Americans depend on every day.

We must also put cooperation ahead of political division. This is a moment that calls for practical solutions, responsible leadership and action—not unnecessary political arguments.

Our priorities are clear: protect the public, restore essential services, safeguard financial confidence and strengthen America’s critical infrastructure against future disruptions.

America has faced difficult challenges throughout its history. By working together and taking the necessary steps, we can move forward.

God bless every American, and God bless the United States of America!” 🇺🇸

Old Flame (Gambler's Folly Book 4) by Mellie Miller is a heartfelt second-chance paranormal shifter romance that blends emotional healing, mature love, and the magic of fate. Billionaire and bear shifter Kort Behrens has been lucky in business but unlucky in love—after two failed marriages and a string of gold diggers, he’s given up hope of finding a real connection. Elizabeth Murphy, a widow for four years, has rebuilt her life through her Reiki practice and the quiet companionship of her cat, Puzzle, still carrying the quiet ache of a long marriage that never fully satisfied her deeper desires. When these old college friends (who never dated) unexpectedly reunite on the way to the enchanted world of Gambler’s Folly, sparks fly and a full-blown romance blooms. Will they seize this second chance at a happily-ever-after, or will doubts and fears snatch it away? On Gambler’s Folly, every love story is a gamble—and Fate always deals the final hand. A slow-burn friends-to-lovers tale full of heart, sensuality, and the series’ signature fantasy charm.

About the author
Mellie Miller first fell in love with writing in a high school creative writing class. Married to her one and only, Steve, they began their journey through life in 1976 and, after two children and many moves, she finally has the time to devote to this love. She mainly writes fantasy romance, often with a paranormal twist, though she also has a short book sharing her struggle with breast cancer. Mellie feels her background in music, martial arts (2nd-degree black belt), and Reiki gives her a broad palette to draw on for her character development. Many of her stories incorporate one or more of these talents. As a lover of fantasy, Mellie hopes the worlds and stories she creates will give others a bit of escape from the hectic world around us and offer hope for a happy outcome. She and her husband live in rural Georgia and share their lives with cats, dogs, and a flock of chickens. She also writes under the pen name Sultonna Nadine.

The Riverwalk is bringing the energy of the NFL to the heart of Southbank: transformed into a high-energy fan zone known as Rams House: The LA Tailgate Experience. As the city welcomes thousands of visitors for a season expected to deliver significant tourism and economic activity, Crown will activate across every major sporting code, offering exclusive fan experiences, iconic events, and world-class hospitality all under one roof.

Netflix has ordered a series set in Las Vegas from three people who know the territory well: Casino director Martin Scorsese and Ocean’s Thirteen writers and Billions co-creators Brian Koppelman and David Levien.

Casino Notes

Casino (TV series / mini-series) Casino (1995–1997):

A famous five-part American television mini-series directed by Martin Scorsese, sometimes referred to as the “Casino trilogy/series” informally because it completes Scorsese’s unofficial mafia trilogy (along with Goodfellas and Casino the movie). However, it’s not actually a traditional TV series but a long-form film released in parts in some countries.

More commonly, people just mean the 1995 film Casino itself when they say “Casino series”

News

Casino (1995) – Martin Scorsese Film & Its Informal "Series"

The iconic 1995 film Casino directed by Martin Scorsese, starring Robert De Niro, Joe Pesci, and Sharon Stone, is often grouped with Scorsese’s other mafia/gangster films as an unofficial trilogy:

Goodfellas (1990)

Casino (1995)

The Irishman (2019)

Fans and critics frequently refer to these three as Scorsese’s “Casino trilogy” or “mob series,” even though they are not direct sequels.

News

Casino (2005–2006) – A short-lived Norwegian drama series about a group of friends running an illegal poker club.

Las Vegas (2003–2008) – NBC series starring James Caan and Josh Duhamel set in a fictional Las Vegas casino (the Montecito). Often what people mean when they say “casino series” in the 2000s context.

Tilt (2005) – ESPN drama about professional poker players trying to take down a corrupt card room boss.

Luck (2012) – HBO series created by David Milch, set at a California racetrack with heavy gambling elements (cancelled after one season).

Classic Dramas and Crime

Casino (1995): Directed by Martin Scorsese, this epic crime film stars Robert De Niro as a gambling associate sent by the mob to oversee operations in Las Vegas.

The Cincinnati Kid (1965): A classic poker film featuring Steve McQueen as an up-and-coming player attempting to take down a legendary master.

The Gambler (1974 / 2014): Both versions follow a literature professor with a self-destructive gambling addiction that leads to dangerous encounters with criminals.

California Split (1974): Directed by Robert Altman, this film is highly regarded for its realistic portrayal of the gambling lifestyle and the friendship between two bettors.

Heist and High-Stakes Action

Ocean’s Eleven (2001): A stylish heist movie where Danny Ocean (George Clooney) and his team attempt to rob three Las Vegas casinos simultaneously.

Casino Royale (2006): James Bond (Daniel Craig) must defeat a private banker to terrorists in a high-stakes poker game at the Casino Royale in Montenegro.

21 (2008): Based on a true story, this film follows the MIT Blackjack Team as they use card counting to win millions from Las Vegas casinos.

Modern Poker and Psychological Thrillers

Rounders (1998): Often credited with fueling the early 2000s poker boom, it stars Matt Damon as a reformed gambler who returns to high-stakes underground games to save a friend.

Molly’s Game (2017): Based on the true story of Molly Bloom, an Olympic-class skier who ran the world's most exclusive high-stakes poker game.

The Card Counter (2021): A crime drama starring Oscar Isaac as an ex-military interrogator turned low-stakes gambler who uses the casino circuit to help a young man seeking revenge.

text:
If there was ever a fight where you rooted for both guys to win, this may have been it:

WBC Super Featherweight Champion Alexis Arguello (Dark trunks) stops challenger Bobby Chacon after seven rounds, on November 16, 1979, at The Forum in Inglewood, California.

UPI reported:

"At the opening bell, Alexis Arguello had a look of supreme confidence. Five rounds later, slightly bruised and behind on all judges scorecards, Arguello exuded even more confidence. Arguello was rocked by the game Bobby Chacon in the first five rounds. The challenger lunged at the champion and scored frequently with lefts and rights. Chacon appeared to hurt Arguello in the 4th round with two looping right hands, but the champion kept backing up, staying out of range, and weathered the attack. The WBC super featherweight champion knew he had taken the best challenge Bobby Chacon had to offer. Now it was his turn. So Arguello came on in the 6th round, hammering Chacon and opening a two inch gash near the corner of Chacon's right eye. In the 7th round, Arguello landed a blistering left hand, dazing Chacon. The challenger retreated to a neutral corner, crouched with his hands on the ropes and took a mandatory eight count, trying desperately to allow time for the bells to stop ringing in his head. At the end of the 7th round, the ring doctor examined Chacon's bloodied eye, stepped back and signaled the end."

Arguello; classy as always, this guy should have given sportsmanship lessons to the entire sport, was complimentary (as usual) of his opponent afterwards, saying:
"From the beginning I said Chacon was a good fighter. He's an intelligent guy and a good boxer. You have to take your time against him."

How refreshing to hear a boxer compliment his opponent in that fashion. The sport could surely use some Arguello's and Chacon's nowadays.

Undefeated Ruben Castillo (43-0) is next for the champ.

For the ever resilient Chacon, a third meeting with Rafael "Bazooka" Limon is next.

text:
Your plan is not working. The November 13 nationwide ground stop was caused by a routine copper-to-fiber cutover performed by the same long-time contractor (L3Harris) that has run the FAA’s aging telecom backbone for more than two decades. 

That single remote site in Arkansas flooded the network because the underlying architecture is still the 1980s system Duffy says he is modernizing. 

Seventy percent of the copper may be replaced, but the live network still has old routers, limited diversity, and single points of failure—exactly the conditions that produce cascading outages during transitions.

Duffy has not been transparent on the actual facts. He has framed the outage as an unavoidable consequence of “historic underinvestment” and a forced copper retirement while downplaying that the work was part of the modernization already under way with the existing contractor. 

He has not addressed why a free Starlink backup offer for precisely this transition window was declined, nor has he reconciled GAO findings that the accelerated “Brand New Air Traffic Control System” effort lacks an integrated master schedule and full lifecycle cost estimate and is prioritizing speed at the risk of further disruptions. 

Continuing to task the same contractor that owns and operates the fragile legacy network with sequential cutovers on the live system is structurally destined to produce more of the same failures.

The work can proceed with lower disruption risk if the new network is built and validated in parallel, satellite/wireless diversity is used as a bridge for remote and transitional sites, and change control is tightened—rather than relying solely on sequential upgrades of the live copper-era backbone. 

Duffy’s current approach does none of those things at scale.
