Stephen A. Smith Presses Abdul El-Sayed on Israel’s Right to Exist as a Jewish State — El-Sayed Fires Back, “Does Palestine Have That Same Right?”

Stephen A. Smith: "With growing concern on antisemitism, do you believe Israel has a right to exist as a Jewish state?”

Abdul El-Sayed: “I believe Palestinians and Jewish Israelis deserve equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination. Our tax dollars shouldn't be used to prevent Palestinians from having that right.

“We're sending billions to a foreign government while children here attend underfunded schools and communities need better healthcare and roads. My responsibility as Michigan's senator would be to serve the people of Michigan.

“If Palestinians and Israelis agree on a two-state solution, fine. If they choose another arrangement, that's for them to decide.”

Stephen A. Smith: “I understand your intentions, but I'm asking a direct question. Do you support Israel's right to exist as a Jewish state? Yes or no?”

Abdul El-Sayed: “You're getting to the heart of the issue. People ask whether Israel has a right to exist, but nobody asks whether Palestine has that same right.

“We've supported a two-state solution for years, yet we're funding an Israeli government that I believe is working to prevent a Palestinian state from existing.

“The real question should be how we guarantee self-determination and security for both Jewish Israeli and Palestinian children.

“We need a system that allows both communities to decide their future, rather than starting with assumptions about what a Jewish state must look like.” https://t.co/S4PnqsoxKB

**Yes.** St. Augustine (354–430) both affirmed and participated in the offering of the Eucharistic sacrifice (the Mass) for the dead.

He describes this as an ancient, universal practice of the Church handed down from the Fathers. In works such as *De cura pro mortuis gerenda* (*On the Care to Be Had for the Dead*), Sermon 172, *City of God* (e.g., 21.24), and the *Enchiridion*, he states that the dead are helped by “the prayers of the holy Church, and by the salvific sacrifice, and by the alms which are given for their spirits.” He notes that the whole Church commemorates those who died in the communion of the Body and Blood of Christ “in their own place in the sacrifice itself; and the sacrifice is offered also in memory of them, on their behalf.” He also references the practice of offering sacrifice for the dead in the books of Maccabees as consistent with the Church’s custom, even while stressing that the Church’s living tradition provides independent authority for it.

Personally, this appears in the account of his mother, St. Monica. On her deathbed she asked only to be remembered “at the Lord’s altar.” In *Confessions* Book 9, Augustine prays for her (and his father Patricius) and urges readers to do the same at the altar, recognizing the holy sacrifice offered there as the means by which sins are blotted out.

As a bishop, Augustine would have offered the liturgy in which such commemorations of the faithful departed regularly occurred. He carefully distinguishes that these offerings benefit those who died in a state where they can still be helped (not the very good who need no further help, nor the very bad for whom they cannot avail), while affirming their efficacy for the rest.

This is fully consistent with the broader early Christian practice of offering the Eucharist for the departed, attested well before Augustine.

text:
There’s an alternate perspective on depression that offers opportunity rather than defeat…

Consider this a period of ‘compression’ rather than ‘depression.’

Using a different word can help you shift to the different understating of this period of your life.  

Compression is an opportunity for you to become more of who you really are. It’s a state that gets triggered by a part of you that’s realized you are not being yourself.

Part of you is taking control of the system and boldly proclaiming:

“Hold up! Stop everything! THIS IS NOT YOU. You haven’t been you for a long time. We can’t continue in this direction. Let’s pause and figure out who you want to be moving forward — because THIS isn’t working for you any more.”

As we go through life we can easily take on a series of fear-based beliefs as a protective armor against the things that have hurt us before.

You’re perhaps at the point where the armor has gotten so thick and heavy that you can’t move. The armor is no longer protecting you, and is the thing that’s killing you. It’s time to take the armor off.

Compression is the breaking point where you decide whether you want to start taking the armor off so you can continue on your journey, or you want to lay down and die encased in a shell of fear. The latter often sounds amazing when in this state. But you don’t need to die. You just need to stop not being yourself. It’s the false version of yourself (you plus the armor) that needs to die.

The armor is built on beliefs such as:

“I screwed up too bad. It’s unforgivable. I’m not worthy of forgiveness, so I will choose to not forgive myself to make sure I am never forgiven.”

“I’m not worthy of being loved. I have no value. Anyone who says they love me therefore must be lying. It’s not possible to love me. I am surrounded by liars who only pretend to love me.”

“If I act the way I want to act, people will dismiss me, hate me, mock me, or leave me.”

“If I do what I want to do, I might feel humiliated. Humiliation is the worst possible experience. I would rather be dead than embarrassed. I will hide and live as if dead to avoid humiliation.”

These are just examples, but the idea is that you may have buried yourself in an overwhelming amount of rules and regulations set up to protect you from being hurt. But all of those rules have forced you to behave as somebody who is not actually you, and that’s what kills the spirit. 

The goal of life is to become as much of yourself as possible in the midst of a world full of people telling you to be who THEY prefer you to be.

Have you ever felt like you just want to be able to pause the whole world? 

Just freeze everything! Freeze time! Give me a second to catch my breath and not have to owe people my time or emotions or love or comfort! Just stop and let me breathe for a second!

If you’ve felt this enough, then this state of compression is the response, the answer. You just haven’t perceived it this way yet. 

Recognize or redefine it as an opportunity. 

Hear me out: lean into it!

All that’s happening is that everything that is not YOU is being reduced in priority so that you can see what’s left over…

What’s left over when there’s nothing outside of you worth keeping up the performance for?

Begin observing yourself.

Literally talk to yourself in your head:

“Dude, when was the last time you were happy?”

I don’t remember.

“Ok that’s fine. When was the last time you felt like yourself?”

Not sure.

“All good! What were you doing the last time you got distracted from the depression for a bit?”

Chatting about shared interests with a coworker for like an hour…

“Oh cool! Let’s remember that and see if there are more opportunities to do that!

…

You’re in a period of self-audit. But if you don’t define it that way, you can’t utilize the opportunity. Recognize it. Take ownership of it. Explore yourself. Make your way back to the world, but come back as YOU. 

Find out how to not be afraid of being YOU. 

Love you!

text:
🇫🇷 La France Insoumise unveiled last week Jean-Luc Mélenchon's platform for the 2027 presidential election. Here are the main proposals:

🔹 Work and wages

➤ Raise France's minimum wage to €1,700 a month after taxes, up €220 from here it currently stands

➤ Repeal President Emmanuel Macron's 2023 reform that raised the retirement age to 64, then restore retirement at 60 with a full pension after 40 years of work

➤ Cut the standard workweek from 35 to 32 hours, starting with physically demanding and night jobs

➤ Cap pay within any company so the top earner makes no more than 20 times the lowest-paid worker

➤ Raise public-sector salaries by 10%

🔹 Taxing the rich

➤ Cap inheritances at €12 million, taxing anything inherited above that at 100%

➤ Scrap inheritance tax entirely on inheritances under €150,000

➤ Bring back the wealth tax on large fortunes that Macron abolished in 2018, adding a levy on major polluters

➤ Impose a "Zucman tax," named after economist Gabriel Zucman, guaranteeing that people worth over €100 million pay at least 2% of their wealth each year

➤ Expand income tax from 5 brackets to 14, so top earners pay more

🔹 Health and cost of living

➤ Have France's public health insurance cover 100% of medical costs, and cover therapy for anyone under 26

➤ Let workers take up to 3 sick days without a doctor's note, and give 7 days of bereavement leave after a friend's death

➤ Freeze prices on essentials like food, energy and fuel, and freeze rents

➤ Raise housing assistance by 10%

➤ Guarantee young people (18-25) an income of €1,337 a month, the poverty line, and offer students €1 meals

🔹 Climate

➤ Create a mandatory 9-month environmental service for under-25s, paid at the minimum wage

➤ Gradually phase out nuclear power, which supplies most of France's electricity, and reach 100% renewable power by 2060

➤ Ban flights between 11 p.m. and 6 a.m.

➤ Suspend low-emission zones that bar older, more polluting cars from city centers, which critics say punish low-income drivers

➤ Cut off public aid to companies that don't meet social and environmental commitments

🔹 Democracy and Revolution

➤ Replace the Fifth Republic, whose 1958 constitution concentrates power in the presidency, with a "Sixth Republic" drafted by an elected assembly

➤ Abolish Article 49.3, which lets the government force laws through parliament without a vote, as Macron's governments repeatedly did

➤ Require police recruits to complete anti-discrimination training

➤ Recognize the Oct. 17, 1961, massacre, when Paris police killed scores of Algerian protesters, many thrown into the Seine, as a state crime

➤ Grant independence to Kanaky–New Caledonia, a French-ruled Pacific territory, on Jan. 1, 2028

🔹 Foreign policy - NATO

➤ Immediately pull French forces out of NATO's integrated military command, the joint structure that puts allied troops under NATO commanders, as President Charles de Gaulle did in 1966, while staying in the alliance for now
 ➤ Then gradually leave NATO altogether, arguing France should be "nonaligned" and not tied to US-led wars
 ➤ Refuse NATO's new target for members to spend 5% of their GDP on defense

🔹 Foreign policy - additional

➤ Renegotiate EU treaties and refuse to apply EU rules that conflict with the program

➤ Suspend the EU-Israel Association Agreement, the deal that gives Israel preferential trade access to Europe

➤ Back a Palestinian state with sovereignty over all territory Israel has occupied since 1967

The futures markets on @Bybit_Official , @binance  and FTX were huge during the 2021 bull run, and that trend has carried on. Even though I wasn't taking on much risk, I still felt the punch when FTX went down and I couldn't get my funds out of BlockFi. The message was clear to me, and to @HyperliquidX 's founder Jeff Yan: decentralised finance was the way forward. That's why I'm excited to cover Hyperliquid's success in today's article.

Why Hyperliquid could be crypto's best project right now

Perps are insanely profitable to run. Hyperliquid has emerged as the highest-earning crypto project of 2026, and the protocol is pushing $1 billion in annual revenue. During the Iran conflict in March, as energy prices spiked, its oil contract hit nearly $1.7 billion in daily trading volume, and weekend commodity volume set a record of $720 million.
Hyperliquid is meeting the modern world's demand for 24/7 trading. Personally, older systems like Interactive Brokers feel clunky. Hyperliquid feels far more intuitive and modern.

What is Hyperliquid?

Hyperliquid describes itself as "Markets for crypto, commodities, indices, and FX. Open 24/7 onchain, without intermediaries." But you're actually trading the price; you don't own the asset itself. So is this the future of derivatives trading?

At its core, Hyperliquid is a decentralised exchange for perpetual contracts, built on its own Layer 1 blockchain. FYI, futures are an obligation to settle at a set price, and they have an expiry date. Perps are futures with no expiry. That's the direct comparison. You use them to bet on a price going up or down, usually with leverage. Binance and Bybit made perps hugely popular, but (cough cough) they're centralised, meaning the company holds your money. Hyperliquid gives you the same fast trading with an order book, while your funds and every trade stay on-chain.

This is the key difference from FTX. At FTX, your balance was just a number in the company's internal system, and nobody outside could see that customer deposits were being moved to Alameda. On Hyperliquid, every deposit, order, trade and liquidation is recorded publicly on the blockchain. Anyone can check that the money is there. Hyperliquid has bridged the gap: it offers the speed of perps on Binance, FTX or Interactive Brokers, but in a decentralised way.

Most decentralised exchanges, like @Uniswap , run on top of a general-purpose chain like Ethereum, which is slow and expensive for high-frequency trading. Hyperliquid went the other way. Its developers call it purpose-built infrastructure for trading valuable assets on a fast, low-cost blockchain ledger. So many crypto projects try to be the Swiss Army knife of crypto and do everything, like ICP (and we all know about their traction). Hyperliquid is just trying to do one thing really well, and it's executing successfully.

@HyperliquidX  Labs was founded by Harvard classmates Jeff Yan, a former high-frequency trader, and iliensinc. It is entirely self-funded and has not taken any money from venture capitalists, which is a flex considering its market cap is over $21 billion. Jeff speaks a lot about FTX in interviews, and how that whole incident opened the door to decentralised finance. He also talks about Hyperliquid reinvesting its profits back into the project rather than taking them. The HYPE token launched in late 2024 with a large airdrop to users and nothing set aside for VCs, which earned it a lot of goodwill.

Token economics and treasury (the bit you'll probably find most interesting)

According to DefiLlama, Hyperliquid's primary form of value accrual is buybacks, which means value flows to the token through buybacks and token burns.
Nearly all of the exchange's trading fees go into an on-chain fund that buys HYPE on the open market. In effect, it's like a company putting almost all its revenue into share buybacks, automatically and in public. At times those buybacks have outpaced new tokens being issued, with reports that Hyperliquid turned deflationary. That direct link between platform usage and token demand is the main reason HYPE is treated as one of the few tokens backed by real cash flow. All fees go to the community, and none are collected by the Hyperliquid team. The protocol has generated north of $900 million in fees from platform usage.
There is also a separate company listed on the US Nasdaq exchange called Hyperliquid Strategies (ticker: PURR). It isn't run by the Hyperliquid team. It's a treasury vehicle designed to buy and stake HYPE tokens, and it holds hundreds of millions in cash.

Perps vs the stock market

Do you own NVIDIA if you buy it through Hyperliquid? No. It's a cash-settled contract that tracks NVIDIA's price. Someone trading a perpetual linked to a listed stock doesn't receive dividends, voting rights or legal ownership in the company. Behind the scenes, NVDA-PERP tracks NVIDIA's spot share price via the @tradexyz  oracle, with hourly funding settlement. An oracle is a data feed that brings the real-world price on-chain.
Funding rate. A perp has no expiry, so something has to keep its price close to the real price. That's the funding rate, a small payment between longs and shorts. On Hyperliquid it's paid every hour. If the perp trades above the real price, longs pay shorts, which pulls it back down, and vice versa. Holding a position for months means paying or earning funding the whole time.
Leverage. Up to 20x on @nvidia . That's great until a 5% move wipes you out.
24/7. NVIDIA perps trade on weekends and overnight, when the Nasdaq is closed.

Concerns

Could the exchange undermine how oil prices are set? Could it chip away at the benchmarks that producers, airlines and traders rely on to price things like oil or petrol? The concern is that prices from this "unregulated investment vehicle" could seep into traditional markets. It could also allow anonymous international traders to undermine Western sanctions. Basically, it's a threat to price integrity.

Another concern is insider coordination, since the platform is permissionless. Hyperliquid is making it clear that it isn't hiding. Its counter-argument is that the platform is more transparent, because every trade, order and liquidation is publicly verifiable on the blockchain. I agree with this, but I also see the risk of anonymous users who are connected to companies, or who have insider information, profiting from the platform. KYC in this part of decentralised finance is important to stop the rich from taking advantage of their power.
Is @HyperliquidX  really decentralised?
Dominic Williams, the founder of ICP (a competitor, it's worth noting), recently argued on X that Hyperliquid is really a centralised exchange. He compared it to the NYSE, which sells hedge funds direct connections to its servers so they can trade faster than everyone else. What Williams is really getting at is that Hyperliquid is starting to behave like a traditional exchange operator, selling privileged access.

His post was a response to a Bloomberg report about Wintermute. A market maker keeps an exchange running smoothly. It constantly posts offers to both buy and sell an asset, so whenever you click "buy" or "sell" there's someone on the other side. It earns a sliver from the gap between its buy and sell prices (the "spread"), repeated millions of times a day. Without market makers, you'd get thin markets: big gaps between prices, and large orders that move the price sharply against you. That's why they matter so much, especially for smaller altcoins.
@wintermute_t  is one of the biggest market makers in crypto. It's a London-based trading firm founded in 2017 by Evgeny Gaevoy, who previously worked at Optiver, a traditional high-frequency trading firm. Think of Wintermute as crypto's version of Citadel Securities or Jane Street. Hyperliquid runs an open auction for early access to order data, and Wintermute is winning most of it: about 76% of the top-priority auctions over the past month.

Why is that a concern?
It sees your order before it's filled. When you place a trade, the top bidder gets to see it about 60 milliseconds before the exchange processes it. That's nothing to a human, but plenty of time for a computer to react.
It undercuts the whole pitch. Part of Hyperliquid's appeal is that it's fairer than old-school finance and FTX. Selling speed to the highest bidder is exactly what traditional exchanges do, which is Williams' point.
So although Hyperliquid is more transparent, that doesn't necessarily make it more equal.

Conclusion
@HyperliquidX  is the most successful project in crypto right now. It generates roughly $800 million to over $1 billion in annualised revenue, according to metrics tracked by @DefiLlama  and @CoinMarketCap  Academy. What's so impressive is that the project runs in a largely decentralised way, which is paving the way for decentralised finance as a whole and taking power away from big players like Binance and Bybit. In a trading world that doesn't want to stop for weekends or holidays, the platform meets the needs of the modern world.

Over how? Over why?

Look at Canada, its national police force could shut down a lemonade stand right now. Its whole army couldn’t pacify the average amateur hockey game. Not exaggerating.

Newton’s third law of motion and Stormy’s 2nd law of political physics:

text:
The room that was worth an empire: November 16, 1532 🏔️

On this day, Francisco Pizarro and just 168 Spaniards sprang an ambush in the town square of Cajamarca, Peru, and captured the Inca emperor Atahualpa, even though his army camped nearby vastly outnumbered them. 

According to Spanish accounts, the only Spaniard wounded was Pizarro himself, who cut his hand stopping one of his own soldiers from killing the emperor. 

Atahualpa then made a legendary offer for his freedom. He would fill a room about 22 by 17 feet with gold, as high as he could reach (about 8 feet), and fill it twice more with silver. Believe it or not, the treasure really arrived, and melting it down into bars took about a month, so very few Inca masterpieces survived. 

Pizarro had Atahualpa executed anyway in 1533.

text:
A little more on my WTF Moriah ’cast appearance, including how those shoutouts came about.

We covered a lot of ground.

Facebook ads. Charlotte, by the way, Moriah sticks to the One Dollar Daily  approach. We talked about how giving FB more money just gives it more room to push your book beyond the audience you set and how one should never fall for their “if you spend more…” nonsense. That is a money churn. 

Amazon ads. We discussed why they’re a waste of money for indie authors. The big publishing houses have their Amazon storefronts, and that is Amazon’s priority. Amazon is glad to churn through our ad budgets, but its focus is catering to the big houses. Their ads get the placement at the right time of day, in the right place. The indie author ads are just a waste of money. But hey, if you want your " impression" at 3AM  when everybody is sleeping, give them your money. They will gladly take it from you.

Posting about low sales on X. We discussed authors lamenting their lack of sales and how the natural reaction for a potential reader is going to be “If nobody else is buying it, why would I?” We talked about how e that kind of post does do anything except  work against you.

Getting a book onto a syllabus. I discussed reaching out to colleges and universities. It’s something I do, and my books are required reading in English courses at several colleges. Colleges rip off students on books, and you can charge colleges an insane amount of money to have author copies shipped to the school bookstores. One college sold my book to students for $40. When I learned this, I charged them $20 per copy on the next order, which is far above the list price on platforms. There isn’t any royalty split, so the markup is all yours. For me it was $15.10 per copy after author copy cost.  We also discussed speaking at colleges to the classes that have your book as required reading. I do this a few times every semester.  

Limitations on categories. The ’Zon, B&N, and the rest give only so many boxes to check. We discussed how books about relationships aren’t necessarily “romance,” but authors are forced to check that box because that’s the closest choice offered.

Moriah pushed back at me about buying books from you people and not reading them. My position remains that “support” is buying. I can’t read everything. I have a globally operating business to run. I barely have enough time to get kittens out of trees, help the elderly cross busy urban boulevards, rescue supermodels from peril, and keep the world safe for democracy.
And some of you folks write things that do not interest me. That does not mean I don’t “support.” I have them shipped to friends and family who read your genre. 

How the shoutouts came about:

We were discussing genres, and the convo went from how erotica is erotica and smut isn’t , "relationship"  books are not  necessarily" romance" to what I read. I mentioned that I don’t read so-called sci-fi fiction, but I did buy @AuthorGoodwin  books. ( I may have mentioned reading @R_R_Hutchinson , I do not recall)

I gave a shoutout to  Barbara of @BCB_Designs  when we were discussing the endless barrage of shitty Canva covers authors make.

The shoutout to  @E_R_A_writes  came about because we were discussing “knowing who your readers are.” I remembered watching Elizabeth on a podcast when she was in England. She said, “Know who your readers are and who they aren’t.” That line stuck with me, which is amazing, seeing as I was basically mesmerized by her presence and still managed to remember one thing she said. As well she was generous enough to send me a signed copy of one her books , I will forever cherish my  signed copy of " The Alewives"

I intended to give a shoutout to @NicholsonS9960  (I had it right there on the index card beside my MacBook), but the convo never got around to poetry.
Moriah wants me back as a guest for my next release( March '27) , I'll make sure to get  the shoutout in on that episode, Stacy ! 

Enywho, this post has churned through my allotted daily ten minutes of X time… Have a great evening, everyone!

text:
KYIV BRIDGES HIT, MAJOR ATTACK REPORTED ON KERCH BRIDGE, TANKER ALERTS IN THE STRAIT OF HORMUZ

World Conflict Live 24/7 | End-of-day report | Monday, November 16, 2026
Good evening. Here’s where today’s major stories stand through 9:55 p.m. Eastern.

UKRAINE AND RUSSIA

A late-day report described a large ballistic missile attack against Ukraine. Kyiv Mayor Klitschko said Russian strikes hit the city’s Northern and Southern bridges. A separate report named Iskander-M ballistic missiles and Zircon hypersonic missiles in a Kyiv bridge strike.

In Dnipro, regional officials said a drone struck a roadway Monday morning, setting cars on fire. 1 person was killed. The initial report put the number of injured at 10, all of whom were hospitalized. 2 men, ages 26 and 47, were in serious condition. Officials later raised the injury count to 13. The day’s attacks also damaged apartment buildings and vehicles.

Separate strikes hit energy facilities in the Dnipro region. Ukrainian energy company DTEK said the entire city lost power. Crews began restoring electricity to water and heating systems and other essential facilities first.

A strike also set fire to the Oleina sunflower oil plant in Dnipro. Its U.S. owner, Bunge, confirmed the strike, said no employees were injured and temporarily suspended operations at the plant.

In Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region, crews ended a two-week search in Komyshuvakha. The confirmed death toll from the November 2 airstrike stood at 72. The strike hit a school where residents had come to collect humanitarian aid. Those killed included rescuers, police, medical staff, utility workers and school staff. One was a teacher who gave online lessons from the shelter to children who had evacuated.

4 people remain missing and 4 are still hospitalized. Ukraine’s Interior Ministry said Russian forces struck the search site 9 times during the operation, injuring 3 police officers and 4 rescuers.

At the Kerch Bridge linking Russia and occupied Crimea, the Kremlin initially reported an overnight Ukrainian drone strike. Road traffic was briefly halted while trains continued to run. The Kremlin described the damage as minor, and no injuries were reported.

Russian occupation authorities in Crimea later confirmed a new overnight strike. Further reports said a span was gone and that more than 15 strikes had been observed at the bridge.

A report received at 9:55 p.m. Eastern described a large-scale Ukrainian missile and drone attack on the Kerch Bridge as ongoing. It said at least 10 cruise missiles and 25 drones had struck the bridge.

Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down a record 2,049 Ukrainian drones in 24 hours and intercepted 4 long-range Flamingo cruise missiles and 7 guided bombs. Later, early reports put a new wave of Ukrainian drones over Russia at more than 400, an unverified figure.

As Moscow came under heavy drone attack, Mayor Sobyanin said 142 drones had been shot down. All of the capital’s airports were reported closed at the time.

In southern Russia, the Rostov regional governor said an overnight Ukrainian drone attack started fires at 4 industrial sites in Azov. 3 men were injured and hospitalized. ASTRA reviewed footage and located one fire near 2 oil depots.

Another report said Ukrainian forces struck the Ilsky oil refinery, hitting its AT-4, AT-5 and AT-6 oil processing units and a gasoline production complex. The refinery can process about 6.6 million tons of oil a year.

In Salavat, Bashkortostan, local residents reported a Ukrainian attack and a fire at the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat petrochemical complex.

BLACK SEA RESCUE AND SHIPPING ALERTS

Off Bulgaria, a rescue operation was launched after the crew of the Somali-flagged cargo ship BETUL 8 reported it was sinking about 40 nautical miles southeast of Cape Kaliakra. Bulgaria’s Transport Ministry said the ship was carrying wheat from Romania to Egypt with 12 people aboard. Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey dispatched 4 ships, and Bulgarian aircraft joined the search.

Bulgarian broadcaster bTV reported that the crew took to life rafts. Their condition and the cause of the emergency remained unclear.

Romania deployed 2 Navy bomb disposal teams after a French Atlantique 2 patrol aircraft spotted 2 drones drifting off the Romanian coast on November 15. One team was checking drone parts for explosives from a Coast Guard vessel about 45 nautical miles east of Mangalia. A second team was aboard a minesweeper heading toward Sfântu Gheorghe. That drone was first spotted about 53 nautical miles east of Chituc. The French crew was flying a NATO deterrence mission from Romania. The drones’ origin remains unclear.

Romania also advised ships to route around an area off the Danube Delta after drones struck 3 commercial vessels near the Sulina Canal late Saturday. Officials said 2 ships were hit in Romanian territorial waters. No casualties were reported. The Defense Ministry warned of airborne and floating objects approaching from the north. Transit remains permitted under advisory No. 172/2026, which took effect November 15 and applies until further notice.

STRAIT OF HORMUZ

UK Maritime Trade Operations issued Warning 207-26 after an unidentified projectile struck a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz at 12:58 a.m. Eastern, sparking an engine-room fire. All crew members were accounted for, and no casualties were reported. The extent of the damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. Authorities were investigating, and UKMTO advised ships to proceed with caution and report suspicious activity.

In another UKMTO notice, a third party reported an attack that disabled a tanker and started an engine-room fire 7 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. UKMTO listed the report time as 2:00 p.m. Eastern. The crew was reported safe. The extent of the damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. UKMTO urged caution while authorities investigated.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed 2 more oil tankers caught fire after striking mines on the southern route through the strait. It put the number of tanker fires since Sunday at 6. Its statement gave no vessel names or crew details.

In a separate claim relayed by @Osint613, Iran’s regular navy reported a 4th tanker fire in 24 hours. It said a tanker suffered severe damage after hitting a mine east of the strait and claimed the vessel had switched off its navigation systems in waters Iran calls restricted.

Separately, @hey_itsmyturn reported a blast in the strait. The location and cause remained unclear.

Diplomatic talks continued as Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, left Islamabad for Muscat on Monday evening after meeting Pakistani officials. Those officials said they were awaiting Washington’s response to Iran’s proposal to reopen the strait.

Iranian Army spokesman Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akrami-Nia said it would stay closed until the U.S. accepts Iran’s terms and warned of a stronger response to renewed attacks. He previously claimed Iran controls the strait and could retaliate beyond the region.

IRAN AND U.S. MILITARY DEVELOPMENTS

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy claimed it captured a U.S. MQM-170 drone intact south of Qeshm Island on Monday morning. It said an electronic warfare unit took control of the drone’s guidance system and landed it. The Guards claimed it had been monitoring air defense and electronic warfare systems. They described it as the unit’s 4th capture of that model and the 8th intact drone their forces have captured near the strait.

In a separate claim, the Guards said they shot down a U.S. Army MQ-1C Gray Eagle over Qeshm Island. Iranian state broadcaster IRIB aired footage it said showed the interception.

In southwestern Iran, @hey_itsmyturn reported 2 missile launches from Haftkal in Khuzestan Province. The first was reported at 8:01 a.m. Eastern, or 4:31 p.m. local time. Its destination remained unconfirmed. The second was reported at 3:18 p.m. Eastern.

The same account reported anti-aircraft fire along the road from Andimeshk to Ahvaz, intense air defense activity in Ramhormoz and jet activity over western Tehran. What prompted the activity in Ramhormoz remained unclear, as did the aircraft’s identity and the reason for the activity over Tehran. A report attributed to Iran’s semi-official Mehr News Agency said air defenses were activated in Isfahan.

Iran is also facing pressure on its natural gas supply ahead of winter. i24NEWS reported that Israel’s security cabinet was told Sunday that shortages could leave Iranian families struggling to heat their homes and add pressure to the economy. Reuters cited Iran’s national gas company as saying wartime damage to 4 processing plants had worsened the shortage. Whether it will trigger protests remains unclear.

U.S. Central Command confirmed the USS Theodore Roosevelt, CVN 71, is operating in its area of responsibility. i24NEWS reported that its arrival brings the number of U.S. aircraft carriers operating in the Middle East to 3 and that about 53,000 U.S. troops are stationed in the region.

The U.S. Army is seeking 17 reinforced-concrete bunkers to replace converted shipping containers used as troop shelters. The plan calls for 10 in Israel, 5 in Saudi Arabia and 2 in Lebanon. The bunkers would offer better protection from indirect fire, including blasts from nearby missile and drone strikes. The Army wants each task order completed within 45 calendar days of award and expects to give contractors 3 days to submit quotes once a formal request is issued.

The Pentagon has recorded 23 U.S. service member deaths in operations tied to the Iran war, attributing 11 to enemy fire and classifying 12 as nonhostile.

In Washington, CNN cited 7 U.S. officials as saying new intelligence suggests Iran is exploring possible attacks on senior Trump administration officials in Washington, D.C. The options reportedly include a dirty bomb or a chemical weapon. CNN said the intelligence identified specific locations and potential targets, prompting U.S. contingency planning. Officials remain divided over whether Iran has the ability or intent to act.

The White House said it is monitoring potential threats and that “at this time there are no credible threats to the homeland.” Iran’s U.N. mission rejected the chemical weapons allegations.

ELSEWHERE IN THE MIDDLE EAST

Israel’s military said it struck a weapons shipment bound for Hezbollah overnight near Janta, in eastern Lebanon’s Beqaa Valley close to Syria. The IDF said the shipment had crossed from Syria into Lebanon and that the area had been used before to move weapons to Hezbollah. Lebanese media described it as the first Israeli airstrike in the area in several months. Lebanon’s National News Agency reported no injuries.

In southern Lebanon, @Osint613 cited Lebanese reports of an Israeli strike on Kfar Tebnit in the Nabatieh area.

In Beirut, U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz urged Hezbollah to hand over its weapons voluntarily, saying, “No country can have two armies.” He met Lebanese President Joseph Aoun to discuss what follows the U.N. peacekeeping mission. Its mandate expires December 31, with withdrawal scheduled through 2027. Waltz said Washington expects U.N. Security Council Resolution 1701, which helped end the 2006 war, to stay in force with some amendments.

In Gaza, the IDF said it demolished a 300-meter tunnel in an Israeli-controlled area near the Yellow Line. It said its Harel Brigade found the tunnel during an ongoing operation against Hamas tunnels and other infrastructure.

In Saudi Arabia, a statement attributed to the Saudi-led coalition said air defenses intercepted and destroyed 2 Houthi drones in the Makkah and Riyadh regions.

In Iraq’s Kurdistan Region, an explosion was reported in Erbil Governorate Monday morning. Separately, Reuters cited 2 security sources as saying sirens sounded at the Khor Mor gas field after a drone flew over the facility.

Iraq and Jordan also banned Telegram on Monday, citing national security concerns, extremist content, cybercrime and other illegal activity.

UNITED STATES

U.S. airlines continued to recover from Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Around 8:00 a.m. Eastern, FlightAware showed 18,531 cancellations and 28,560 delays since Friday, for a total of 47,091 disruptions from multiple causes. Reuters later reported that U.S. air travel had largely returned to normal after more than 18,000 cancellations and nearly 28,000 delays over 3 days.

United Airlines experienced a fresh systemwide IT and operational problem that held up departures Monday. The airline later said it had resolved the issue.

In the Bronx, 2 police officers and a civilian were reportedly shot. Early reports said the suspect was barricaded and the victims’ conditions were unclear. A later update said the suspect was found dead from a self-inflicted gunshot wound and all 3 victims were expected to survive.

New York City announced it was disbanding the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group and setting up a civilian Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division. Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch said the civilian team will be unarmed, have no arrest powers and work with demonstrators and police to ease tensions.

In the interim, 30 uniformed officers will handle dialogue and de-escalation. A separate NYPD patrol unit will support crowd management and make arrests as needed. The reforms also ban tear gas, long guns and kettling, a tactic that confines protesters to a limited area.

In Columbia, Missouri, about 40 to 50 employees evacuated the Kraft Heinz plant on Waco Road after a bomb threat around 5:30 p.m. Central on Sunday. Police and bomb-detection dogs searched the building and found no explosives. Workers were allowed back inside around 10:00 p.m. Central. Police reported no injuries. The investigation remained open Monday, with no suspects in custody. Local station 93.9 The Eagle reported it is the only plant in North America that makes Oscar Mayer hot dogs.

Chase customers reported trouble signing in and viewing balances or transactions. Downdetector logged more than 2,000 reports about Chase by 11:04 a.m. Eastern, and Plaid confirmed a disruption to its Chase connections.

Trackers also recorded reports involving Wells Fargo, Bank of America, U.S. Bank, Capital One and TD Bank. One tracker showed 59 U.S. Bank reports and 113 Capital One reports in separate hourly snapshots. TD Bank users also reported trouble signing in and using the app. The extent of the problems at those 5 banks remained unclear.

In Michigan, veterans and gun owners called for a boycott of Fenix Ammunition following remarks by its owner, Justin Nazaroff. The report said he questioned veterans’ benefits and tax breaks, compared the risks of military service to logging, fishing and roofing, and accused troops of fighting for defense contractors. It described derogatory remarks about veterans and Gold Star widows and inflammatory comments about U.S. troops, race and Jewish people.

The same report said Nazaroff posted what was described as a Nazi salute and threatened to shoot military recruiters if they came to his home to force him into a war involving Israel. Critics pointed to pandemic loans received by his own company, some of which were forgiven. Fenix sells ammunition to customers who include military veterans and has sought business from police departments.

Thanks for following along today. Have a good night, and we’ll see what tomorrow brings.

— World Conflict Live 24/7 | @WCLNews247

Good morning you lovely lot, happy Tuesday everyone! 🎄😂

TUESDAY! MONDAY’S UGLY LITTLE BROTHER!

We’ve survived Monday. Unfortunately, our reward is four more days of getting up when we’d rather be tucked up in bed!

Still, Christmas magic is creeping in. The shops are starting to sparkle, and somewhere a bloke is untangling 400 Christmas lights while questioning his life choices! 🤣

Today’s journey back in time is courtesy of Doc Brown’s DeLorean.

Getting it to 88mph on the M62 proved difficult thanks to roadworks, a caravan doing 43mph and somebody from Leeds overtaking a lorry at walking pace!

GREAT SCOTT! WE’VE LANDED IN 1987! 🤣

WELCOME TO CHRISTMAS 1987! 🎄

38 DAYS UNTIL CHRISTMAS! 🎅

Margaret Thatcher was in Downing Street, Rick Astley was never going to give you up, and children were studying toy adverts harder than their schoolwork!

CHRISTMAS NUMBER ONE! 🎶

The Pet Shop Boys topped the charts with Always on My Mind, beating The Pogues and Kirsty MacColl’s Fairytale of New York.

And who remembers that famous line?

“You scumbag, you maggot, you cheap lousy…”

How many of you just filled in the missing word? 🤣

Or has your brain been reprogrammed quicker than a BBC Radio 1 producer reaching for the censorship button?

SOMEWHERE IN BROADCASTING HOUSE, A COMPLIANCE OFFICER HAS JUST SPILLED THEIR SOYA LATTE! 😂

THE GREAT CHRISTMAS TELLY BATTLE! 📺

Christmas Day 1987, after the Queen’s Speech:

BBC1 — 3:10pm: EastEnders, followed by Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom at 3:40pm.

ITV — 3:10pm: Alice in Wonderland, followed by Bedknobs and Broomsticks at 4:35pm.

Imagine the BBC planning meeting:

“It’s Christmas! Families are together, children are excited, everyone’s full of goodwill. What shall we put on?”

“EASTENDERS! NOTHING SAYS PEACE ON EARTH LIKE FAMILY ROWS AND SOMEBODY CRYING INTO A PINT IN THE QUEEN VIC!” 🤣

Honestly, the BBC could make a Christmas cracker depressing.

You’d pull it, the paper hat would be black, the joke about unemployment and the plastic gift a counselling appointment!

IT’S CHRISTMAS, BBC, NOT A NATIONAL DAY OF MOURNING! 😂

Then Indiana Jones turns up and somebody has their heart ripped out.

AFTER ALBERT SQUARE, THAT PROBABLY COUNTED AS LIGHT ENTERTAINMENT! 🤣

OPERATION MERRY BLOODY CHRISTMAS! 🎄

Today’s target: Christmas television adverts!

Remember when adverts simply told you what was for sale?

Now they’re three-minute Hollywood tragedies involving lonely hedgehogs, grieving snowmen and cheerful songs slowed down until they’re bloody depressing!

I ONLY WANTED TO KNOW IF THE MINCE PIES WERE ON OFFER, NOT HAVE AN EMOTIONAL BREAKDOWN BEFORE THE WEATHER! 😂

Give us some Christmas magic, a proper festive tune and a hearty Merry Christmas!

TODAY’S CHRISTMAS MEMORY! ❤️

Who made Christmas magical when you were little?

Mum cooking enough food for the entire street? Dad secretly eating Father Christmas’s mince pie? Grandparents arriving with enough treats to survive a nuclear winter?

Who made Christmas special for you, and what’s your favourite memory of them? ❤️

AI helps check the historical details. The humour and opinions are mine.

Have a cracking Tuesday, everyone!

Laugh hard. Run fast. Be kind. ♥️

Denver in the Dark and Jeffco Dispatch News
Monday Night Dispatch Update | November 16, 2026 | Approximately 8:40 PM

Emergency crews across the Denver metro area responded to numerous crashes, medical emergencies, fires, and public safety incidents throughout the late afternoon and evening.

Among the more significant reports were a missing juvenile in Wheat Ridge, a possible stabbing or gunshot injury in Littleton, a lithium battery fire in Golden, and multiple vehicle crashes across Jefferson County.

JEFFERSON COUNTY

Wheat Ridge | Missing Juvenile on RTD Bus

8:26 PM | West 38th Avenue and Upham Street

Dispatch received a report of a possible missing juvenile with memory difficulties aboard an RTD Route 38 bus. The girl was described as having blonde hair and wearing brown clothing. Her status has not been confirmed.

Littleton | Possible Stabbing or Gunshot Injury

6:06 PM | South Newland Way

Fire and medical crews were dispatched to a reported traumatic injury, described over dispatch as a possible stabbing or gunshot wound. The nature and severity of the injury remain unconfirmed.

Golden | Lithium Battery Fire Rekindles

8:01 PM | Jefferson County Parkway

Fire crews responded to a reported lithium battery fire involving towels inside a building. The fire reportedly rekindled after initially being extinguished.

Crews removed the battery, monitored air conditions, and ventilated a lower level. Dispatch indicated no medical needs for inmates or staff.

Lakewood | Hit-and-Run Investigation

6:14 PM | Kipling Street and West 11th Avenue

Officers were reportedly searching for a white truck following a possible hit-and-run collision. Dispatch indicated the vehicle may have been registered in Wheat Ridge.

Lakewood | Crash Blocks Multiple Lanes

6:10 PM | West 4th Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard

A reported crash was affecting three of four lanes, prompting discussion of a possible detour. Current lane conditions have not been confirmed.

Lakewood | Additional Vehicle Collisions

5:10 PM | South Valley Boulevard and West Ohio Avenue

Engine 7 and Medic 7 were dispatched to a possible motor vehicle collision.

5:15 PM | Northbound Wadsworth Boulevard

West Metro Fire Rescue responded to a possible single-vehicle crash. Two occupants were reportedly outside the vehicle.

6:00 PM | West 2nd Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard

Dispatch reported a possible vehicle collision.

6:00 PM | West 2nd Avenue near Blackstone or Bluestone Boulevard

Engine 3 and Medic 3 were dispatched to another reported collision. The exact cross street was unclear in the dispatch summary.

Edgewater | Vehicle Collision

5:33 PM | Jay Street and West 26th Avenue

Fire and medical units responded to a reported motor vehicle collision.

Golden | Reported Assault and Injury

4:40 PM | Lookout Mountain Road

Golden | Traumatic Injury

Golden | Medical Emergency

Crews responded to a report of a person possibly unconscious or experiencing a fainting episode.

Golden | Person Enters Train Tunnel

A caller reported flashing red and yellow signals causing confusion among motorists. City officials were to be notified.

Lafayette | Welfare Check

Officers responded to a convenience store after an older man appeared lost and confused. Staff reportedly helped redirect him after he attempted to leave in a vehicle.

Boulder | Reported Assault

6:30 PM | 28th Street

Fire crews were dispatched to a reported assault-related medical emergency involving a woman who had reportedly been struck in the head. Police were already on scene.

Boulder | Damaged Scooter Investigation

6:35 PM | Table Mesa Drive

Responders investigated a damaged scooter with broken handlebars and a report of a possibly intoxicated person. The individual was not located, and units cleared.

Boulder | Suspicious Solicitation

7:22 PM | Habitat Drive

Superior | Erratic Driver

ADAMS COUNTY AND BROOMFIELD

ARAPAHOE COUNTY AND SOUTH METRO

PUBLIC SAFETY NOTE

These incidents are based on publicly available emergency dispatch audio and preliminary automated summaries. They are not official police or fire reports. Details, locations, and outcomes may change as agencies investigate.

Denver in the Dark and Jeffco Dispatch News will continue monitoring developments across the metro area.

I joined Channel NewsAsia to discuss what Southeast Asia wants from President Trump’s upcoming visit to Manila for the ASEAN summit - and why it matters for US interests.

I argued that Washington will find more willing and able partners to achieve its objectives if it takes the region’s interests seriously.

On AI chips, US concerns about China gaining indirect access to restricted computing power are real. But legitimate Southeast Asian projects also face potential delays, higher compliance costs and uncertainty. Without clear rules and predictable licensing, the region’s AI ambitions could suffer.

Critical minerals offer scope for mutually beneficial cooperation. Washington wants to diversify supplies and processing away from China; Southeast Asian countries want investment, technology, and more processing and manufacturing within the region. US tariffs complicate that offer.

The pressures on Southeast Asia extend beyond US-China rivalry. China’s unlawful and coercive actions in the South China Sea and US economic nationalism pose distinct challenges to regional security and prosperity. The war in the Middle East has further strained the region’s economic and energy security.

Washington has spoken of a common destiny with Indo-Pacific countries. Its policies should demonstrate that it believes this - that strengthening Southeast Asia strengthens the United States as well.

📺 Watch the interview: https://t.co/0FGY32zLjy

For months, @SecScottBessent defended selling limited Nvidia chips to China as a way to preserve American technological leadership. He wanted American technology to remain the standard “across the world or even in China,” and dismissed national-security objections: “There are no national security concerns here.” Nvidia’s pursuit of the Chinese market was a strategy he publicly championed. 

So, for him to now turn around and frame @JensenHuang's pursuit of the Chinese market as inherently contrary to American interests--this is simply stunning its sheer cynicism. 

I don't like to use the word gaslighting, but it is hard to resist in this case. 

1. July 15, 2025: 
Bessent argued on Bloomberg TV that blocking Nvidia from selling any chips was self-defeating: "if there’s an equivalent chip, then the Nvidia H20 could be sold."  

Shutting out U.S. suppliers, he warned, risked a Chinese "digital Belt and Road" taking root worldwide as countries substituted Chinese chips for American ones. 

Pressed on whether Washington had traded chip licenses for rare-earth access, Bessent called the April restriction a "negotiating chip that we used in Geneva and in London" and described reopened sales as "part of a mosaic," adding: "They had things we wanted. We had things they wanted." Nvidia wasn't subverting U.S. policy in China; Washington was actively deploying Nvidia's market access as leverage in its statecraft.
https://t.co/PymbIk8kMh

2. August 13, 2025: 
Pressed on whether allowing chip sales in exchange for shared revenue put a price on national security, Bessent dismissed the premise outright: "There are no national security concerns here." He stated the strategic goal plainly: "we do not want the standard to become Chinese across the world or even in China." 

When Bessent that Beijing was discouraging domestic firms from buying the chips, Bessent offered to raise the issue with his Chinese counterpart, reading Beijing's pushback as fear that Nvidia would remain China's technological standard. That is word-for-word the argument @JensenHuang is now vilified for making.
https://t.co/tZyfw2Qhcy

3. November 4, 2025: 
Bessent went further, floating eventual sales of flagship Blackwell chips to China. Once rapid innovation pushed Blackwell several tiers behind Nvidia's newest processors over 12 to 24 months, he concluded: "And at that point, they too could be sold off." Export controls, in his telling, were meant to move upward with the technology.   https://t.co/wfPquUrrek

4. December 8, 2025 – January 15, 2026:
The administration codified conditional exports of the H200—a generation ahead of the H100—as a national-security imperative. Following President Trump's December 8 policy announcement, the Commerce Department unveiled its implementing rule on January 13, quoting Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler: "Permitting the sale of the H200 to China under controlled conditions will strengthen the American technology ecosystem." https://t.co/glKF2PUm9s

The final rule, effective January 15, stated in the Federal Register (91 Fed. Reg. 1686) that its "primary direct benefit is to improve national security." 

Controlled Chinese access to H200 chips was not a loophole; it was formal U.S. national-security policy.
https://t.co/pdHxDQkJXL

5. November 13, 2026:
In a CNBC interview, Bessent begrudgingly admits past licensed sales to China while insisting the administration had drawn a hard line at an H100 ceiling. This is demonstrably false.  Anyone can read the Federal Register and see otherwise: his own administration publicly approved, defended, and codified H200 exports ten months earlier.

https://t.co/JpDcY9E4eD

6. November 13–15, 2026: 
Bessent acknowledged that Jensen's personal knowledge of the alleged diversion of chips to China had not been established: “we don't know for a fact that Jensen Huang knew this.” Yet that did not stop Bessent from calling for “a dramatic shake-up” and insisting that Nvidia “go outside the company” for its next CEO. What's more, Bessent is complaining that Nvidia failed to police a Singapore buyer that his own administration refused to put on the Entity List. Commerce hasn't added a firm to the Entity List since October 2025, when Bessent himself announced a one-year suspension of the anti-circumvention rule extending export restrictions to foreign affiliates. Bessent announced: “Yes, we are going to be suspending that for a year in return for the suspension ...on the rare earth licensing regime.”
https://t.co/ZmGdvkLYFa

Incidentally, BIS subsequently extended the suspension through January 10, 2027, so the pause remained in effect during Bessent’s recent criticism.

🏛️ BABY BOOMERS: THE NEXT BAD GUY —
Who Holds the Deed, Who Owes the Bill, Who Pays 🏠
🧭 THE RECKONING ▸ ▸ ▸ 📖 Post 20 OF 20
You Paid Into Social Security. Where Did the Money Go? | Natalie Brunell... https://t.co/aJHrzyDMeP via @YouTube 

Donna retired in May 2019, at 58. She thought about selling her Denver house and moving somewhere smaller, until she looked at the market. "If I sold my house, I wouldn't be able to replace it," she said.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
PART THREE — WHO PAYS
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

THE WOMAN IN THE AVERAGES

She told her story to Yellow Scene, in a January 2026 piece by Ty Flores. On paper, Donna is a boomer homeowner, part of the generation said to own the country. In practice, she is boxed in. The same article reported that a 9.7 percent rise in Medicare premiums consumed roughly a third of 2026's cost-of-living increase, which averaged about $56 a month.

Nineteen posts tested the talking point she supposedly embodies. This one says what held up, what cannot be proven, and what could fix it.

◆ ◆ ◆

THE PEOPLE IN THIS SERIES

Cinda Gillilan is paying rent in Silver City and doing the math on 2032. The Websters say they cannot pay the taxes on the house they built. Henry Ruhl got a bill for his wife's care weeks after he buried her. Gene Lokken's family paid about $12,000 a month after his insurer decided 19 days was enough. Butch Lewis opened a letter and did not live to see the rescue that carries his name.

Across the table, Jay Washington has three degrees and a coin-flip chance of out-earning his parents, and Brittany Gilroy cannot find a starter home with a down payment in the bank. The talking point describes the average boomer. The bill lands on the median one, and on the young renter beside her.

◆ ◆ ◆

EVIDENCE WE CANNOT PROVE

Some claims cannot be settled by the record. They are listed so silence is not mistaken for proof.

❌ Whether anyone planned to make the boomers the next bad guy. Post 18 documented the blame from several directions, but framing is not proof of coordination.

❌ Whether noncitizen voting changed any 2026 result. State audits find dozens or hundreds per state, and federal claims of hundreds of thousands are unproven.

❌ Whether anyone is building a system to control Americans through their money. Post 17 shows who profits from each swipe and who is shut out when the rails stop. It found no evidence of a plan.

One more is political.

❌ Whether the border wave or the pandemic spending was meant to keep a party in power. Posts 7 and 14 document the policies and costs; the motive is not in the record.

❌ What decades of weight-loss drug use will do to Medicare's budget or patients' health.

Three more questions are argued on the record, and none is settled.

⚖️ Whether the SEC's 2004 rule caused the 2008 collapse. Critics say yes, and the SEC's own trading director said it undid no leverage limits.

⚖️ How much DOGE actually saved. GAO could not verify most of what it reviewed, and no one has published a full accounting.

⚖️ Whether corporate greed and corruption drove the young's decline. The record shows growth flowing unequally, insurers overpaid by MedPAC's estimate, and nine in ten 2026 voters calling corruption a major factor. Proving motive is beyond it.

◆ ◆ ◆

THE READER'S VERDICT

✅ ESTABLISHED
▸ Boomer households hold more housing wealth and net worth than any other generation.

▸ Debt held by the public hit 100 percent of the economy in fiscal 2026, the highest at a fiscal year-end since 1946, on a $2.0 trillion deficit.

▸ The 2008 crisis was officially found avoidable. The banks repaid their rescue, and by ProPublica's count one Wall Street executive went to jail.

▸ The retirement trust fund runs out in late 2032, triggering a 22 percent cut, and the surplus the boomers paid in was lent to the Treasury and spent.

▸ Poverty among Americans 65 and older is the highest of any age group under the Supplemental Poverty Measure, which counts housing and medical costs.

▸ Medicare Advantage is paid about $76 billion more than traditional Medicare would cost in 2026 by MedPAC's estimate, which insurers dispute.

▸ Net interest, $1.142 trillion in fiscal 2026, passed Medicare and the military.

▸ Both parties wrote the bill: Republican tax cuts a Democratic president mostly made permanent, Clinton-signed deregulation, a party-line Democratic rescue law, and Social Security fixes abandoned under Bush and Obama.

▸ Absolute mobility fell from about 90 percent for children born in 1940 to about 50 percent for those born in the 1980s.

📊 STRONG EVIDENCE
▸ Americans 65 and older head about one owner-occupied home in three, per Census figures republished by the home builders.

▸ Investors own about 18 percent of single-family homes under the broadest definition, mostly small owners, per BatchData.

▸ Tax cuts account for a larger share of the debt's rise since 2001 than the 2008 and COVID rescues combined, per the Peterson Foundation.

▸ The top tenth of households hold about four-fifths of government and municipal bonds held directly, per the Fed.

⚖️ DISPUTED
▸ Whether the generational gap is mainly about age or mainly about a broken ladder. The mobility research favors the second.

❌ NOT ESTABLISHED
▸ That boomers own all, or most, of America's homes.

▸ That migrant spending is a major cause of the federal deficit.

▸ That the Pentagon's untrackable $2.3 trillion, or the Social Security surplus, was stolen.

◆ ◆ ◆

THE ROAD BACK

▸ MERGE THE TRUST FUNDS. Combining the retirement and disability funds would move the cliff from late 2032 to 2034 and shrink the automatic cut from 22 percent to 17. It needs Congress and does not close the gap.

▸ RAISE OR LIFT THE PAYROLL TAX CAP. Earnings above $184,500 are untaxed for Social Security in 2026. Seniors' groups favor this route, as did 68 percent of Americans asked by Pew in 2023 about taxing high earners for Social Security and Medicare.

▸ FIX THE OVERPAYMENT. CBO's menu shows that cutting Medicare Advantage benchmarks by 10 percent would save about $615 billion over a decade, and the Republican-led Joint Economic Committee found the overpayment raises Part B premiums for seniors in both kinds of Medicare.

▸ FUND THE BASICS. The FAA says it needs $30 billion more to replace failing equipment. The White House offered about $4 billion.

▸ KEEP CASH WORKING. The Payment Choice Act, with sponsors from both parties, would require businesses to take cash up to $500; it sits in committee.

▸ SHARE THE GROWTH. Chetty's team found that spreading growth as broadly as in the 1940s would reverse more than two-thirds of the mobility decline.

◆ ◆ ◆

EPILOGUE

In a 1983 film, a drug lord stands up in a restaurant and tells the diners they need people like him, so they can point their fingers and say there goes the bad guy.

Every era needs one, and this one has been offered the boomers. After twenty posts, most of the numbers point elsewhere: books the Pentagon still cannot balance, wars on a credit card, a crash its own investigators called avoidable, rescues and tax cuts from both parties, a pandemic that closed Main Street while the giants grew, insurers paid more to cover the old, and growth that stopped reaching the bottom half of every generation. Above both parties sits the money: federal lobbying hit a record $4.4 billion in 2024, and the industries in this series give to both sides.

The boomers are not innocent of the bill. As a generation, they had history's best timing, they collect more than they paid in, and their programs are the budget's largest. But the boomers most likely to pay are not the ones in the averages. They are renters on a single check, and owners like Donna in Denver, holding a house she cannot replace, each facing a check that shrinks in 2032.

Cinda Gillilan named the year, and it is six years away. Whoever holds power then will decide who gets handed the bill, and whether the country says goodnight to a bad guy or to the fiction that it needed one.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
📜 SOURCE METHODOLOGY
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

Census figures appear only as republished by outside groups, chiefly the National Association of Home Builders.

Primary sources include the Federal Reserve's surveys and accounts; Treasury and CBO budget data; GAO reports on TARP, DOGE and insurance; the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission; SEC, FBI and FinCEN records; MedPAC; the Joint Economic Committee; the 2026 Trustees report; NERC and EIA; and peer-reviewed research in JAMA, Science and the Review of Financial Studies.

Company estimates are labeled; advocates are quoted for positions, not proof.

Age groups are under 40, 40 to 61, and 62 and older. Election results follow AP calls and exit polls.

Mr. Boulos, the people of Sudan have heard enough appeals for humanitarian access. What they desperately need is for powerful governments to confront the machinery that keeps their suffering alive.

And since you are discussing Sudan from Abu Dhabi, there is a question that deserves an answer.

How can Washington demand an end to drone attacks while leaving the networks that finance, equip, and sustain Sudan’s armed factions at the center of an unresolved international controversy?

In January 2025, your own Treasury Department identified UAE-based Capital Tap Holding as a supplier of money and weapons to the Rapid Support Forces.

In September 2026, UN investigators documented transnational networks involving individuals and entities operating in the UAE that facilitated military support and the recruitment of foreign fighters.

The UAE denies supporting the RSF. These allegations therefore demand credible, independent investigation and effective enforcement.

Washington has imposed sanctions, including against networks supporting both sides. Those measures matter. But Sudanese families are entitled to ask what has actually changed in the flow of weapons, financing, and military technology.

A humanitarian truce without serious efforts to interrupt the supply chains sustaining the war risks becoming little more than a temporary silence between successive massacres.

The Jeddah process offers an established diplomatic framework. What it needs is enforceable commitments, credible monitoring, and consequences for those who continue enabling atrocities.

Mr. Boulos, you speak of protecting aid workers from deadly drones.

Then follow the drones.

Follow the money.

Follow the procurement networks.

And demand accountability wherever the evidence leads, regardless of whose territory, companies, or political relationships are involved.

The children of El Fasher cannot survive on diplomatic statements. They deserve protection from the weapons that kill them, and justice for the crimes already committed.

Peace will not be measured by the number of meetings held in Abu Dhabi, but by the number of Sudanese lives those meetings help save.

text:
The United States Is Paving the Way for New Wars in the Middle East.

For decades, the United States was the dominant power shaping the Middle East's security order, particularly in the Gulf. Washington maintained military bases, protected its allies, and used its power to contain conflicts that threatened regional stability. Although wars continued to erupt, the presence of a superpower imposed certain limits on the ambitions of regional states. Countries had to consider Washington's response before taking action.

Now, as the United States seeks to scale back its security commitments, Middle Eastern countries are rapidly forming new military alliances. On August 7, 2026, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey signed the Mecca Collective Defense Agreement. Just over three months later, on November 13, Qatar and Turkey signed a separate mutual defense agreement. These successive agreements show how urgently regional states are seeking new security guarantees.

This trend will make the Middle East more unstable. The region is already deeply divided by competing national interests, ethnic and religious differences, and geopolitical ambitions. Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the UAE, Turkey, Iran, Israel, and other countries all pursue their own objectives, sometimes in direct opposition to one another.

As U.S. dominance declines, regional states will face fewer constraints and gain greater freedom to pursue their ambitions. New military alliances offer more security options, but they may also embolden countries to confront their rivals, believing they can count on at least one ally to defend them. More dangerously, a conflict between two countries could draw in several others through collective defense commitments. Alliances created to prevent war could instead cause wars to spread.

The Middle East has never lacked countries seeking greater power and influence. What it lacks is a shared vision of regional security. For decades, the United States maintained a regional order through its overwhelming power. Although far from perfect, that order imposed constraints on competing ambitions, providing what has so far been the most effective barrier against wider regional conflict.

Middle Eastern countries may gain greater strategic autonomy as the United States scales back its role. But greater freedom to pursue national ambitions does not mean greater peace. Without a power strong enough to impose order, the Middle East risks becoming a region where each country sets its own limits on the use of force, and war becomes a means of settling disputes.

text:
Rikki Zagelbaum, Jewish News Syndicate
Working with French Jews to fight antisemitism is a priority for Laurent Ulrich, archbishop of Paris, and Catholics and Jews in the capital exchange messages and hold meetings to grow their “friendship human to human,” he told JNS via a translator at Yeshiva University on Monday.

Ulrich, who became archbishop in 2022, visited Yeshiva’s campus in Washington Heights, in upper Manhattan, as part of a group of 11 Catholic clergy and officials from France, Germany and Rwanda.

He told JNS that his visit to the flagship Modern Orthodox institution wasn’t his first but that more than a decade had passed since his last trip there. He said that he meets often with rabbis and attends annual Holocaust memorials. The local bishop’s conference recently published a booklet that offers parishioners guidance on fighting Jew-hatred, he said.

Fr. Alexandre Comte, national delegate for relations with Judaism at the French Bishops’ Conference who teaches Old Testament to seminarians studying in Paris to become priests, told JNS that he was struck on a tour of the Yeshiva study hall by the volume of Torah study.

“For me, it was the first time in a yeshivah,” he said. “I was surprised when visiting the yeshiva—the noise. It’s very strange to hear all the noise in the study.”

Comte told JNS in Hebrew that Catholics “usually” study “in quiet.” JNS asked in Hebrew how much of the language Comte speaks. “A little,” he said, in Hebrew.
The rise in Jew-hatred in France and across Europe is deeply troubling, he told JNS.

“It is so bad to see in France, and all Europe—the rising of antisemitism,” he said. “I know that in the U.S. also there is a rise of antisemitism, but fortunately, it is not as high as it is in France.”

Fighting antisemitism requires Christians to better understand Judaism, according to Comte.

“It is not possible for Christians to be antisemitic. It’s impossible,” he told JNS. “It is part of our faith to be in relation with the people of Israel.”

“The reason why some Christians have some bad thoughts about Israel comes from ignorance, and we work very hard to help Christians to know better,” he said.

“Every Sunday, we read the Torah,” he told JNS. “In the liturgy of the Mass, the first reading is from the Torah.”

“Every Sunday is an opportunity to explain the word of God and the close relation between the two communities, Christian and Jewish communities,” he said.

Ari Berman, a rabbi and president of Yeshiva, told JNS that Catholic leaders have visited the university periodically for years, dating back to the presidency of the late Norman Lamm.

text:
🧭 ANSE INTENDANCE | TRAVEL ESSENTIALS
📍 Getting There

Located in southern Mahé, around 40–50 minutes by car from Victoria. A rental car or taxi offers the most flexibility, especially when exploring nearby beaches.

Public bus route 5A serves Intendance from Victoria, but departures are limited. Check the latest SPTC timetable and plan your return journey.

🗺️ What to Explore

Walk along the sweeping white-sand beach, admire the Indian Ocean surf, and photograph the tropical coastline.

For a contrasting coastal experience, combine your visit with nearby Anse Takamaka, where the bay is generally more sheltered.

⏱️ Time Needed

Allow 1–2 hours for exploring and photography. A half-day works well when combining several southern Mahé beaches.

🌤️ When to Visit

May–September often brings powerful surf during the southeast trade winds. Conditions are generally calmer during the northwest monsoon season, although strong currents remain possible.

💰 Costs & Local Insight

Lawsuit Settlement on Insider-Trading Case

12/29/2017

(COLUMBUS, Ohio)—Today Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine announced a settlement of $290 million in the insider-trading lawsuit against William A. Ackman, his hedge fund Pershing Square Capital Management LP, pharmaceutical company Valeant Pharmaceuticals International, Inc., and related defendants, on allegations that the defendants violated the insider-trading laws and reaped illicit profits by buying up billions of dollars of shares from unsuspecting Allergan, Inc. investors  who were not privy to Valeant’s plans to acquire Allergan at a significant premium.
 
DeWine filed the case on behalf of the Ohio State Teachers Retirement System (STRS), which was a co-lead plaintiff in the case along with a public employee retirement system in Iowa.   The amount that Ohio STRS will receive from the settlement will be determined as part of the claims administration process. 

“We filed this case to send a message that all investors have to play by the same rules,” said Attorney General Mike DeWine.  

Allergan stockholders alleged that in February 2014, Valeant tipped Pershing Square founder William "Bill" Ackman about its plan to launch a hostile bid for Allergan.  Armed with this nonpublic information, Pershing then bought 29 million shares of Allergan stock from unsuspecting investors, who were unaware of the takeover bid that Valeant was preparing in concert with the hedge fund. When Valeant publicized its bid in April 2014, Allergan stock shot up by $20 per share, earning Pershing $1 billion in profits in a single day.  Valeant’s bid spawned a bidding war for Allergan. The company was eventually sold to Actavis PLC for approximately $66 billion.

The federal securities laws expressly prohibit anyone from trading on nonpublic information about an upcoming tender offer.  The purpose of those laws is to establish a level playing field so that hedge funds and corporate raiders with material inside information about upcoming corporate transactions do not take unfair advantage of investors who do not have access to that inside information.

text:
Rant if anyone cares to read:

C.J. Stroud has slowly but surely, and politely, been asserting himself more this season when it comes to having a voice in the Texans offensive scheme, game plans and play calling.

And while I think that's a GOOD thing, I also think it speaks to some much larger issues with how this organization has handled its franchise quarterback.

A few thoughts:

1. Stroud is increasingly speaking up about what he wants offensively.

We've seen it in his public comments about wanting to be more aggressive, pointing to concepts they've already shown they can execute successfully, and now most recently discussing the need to expand the playbook and route tree to have better answers against certain blitz looks.

We were told Stroud would have more command and control of the offense this season, but how much does he actually have? Is he unable to check into better plays against these looks? Or are the answers they've installed simply not good enough?

Hard to know without being in those meetings, but the results speak for themselves. This offense has repeatedly struggled to adjust when defenses present something different than what was anticipated. Are they not valuing any in-game feedback?

2. Why did it take desperation to start leaning into Stroud's strengths?

Stroud has a very high football IQ IMO and I think his time at Ohio State played a big part in that.

I do give Nick Caley credit for seemingly being more receptive to his input than Bobby Slowik appeared to be.

But it also feels like much of the increased willingness to lean into Stroud has come out of desperation following the 0-4 and 2-5 starts rather than a genuine commitment to building the offense around his abilities from the beginning.

Why does it feel like your 25-year-old quarterback has to continually push for aggressiveness, adjustments and concepts that should already be part of the offensive plan?

3. This raises bigger questions about the organization's entire approach to Stroud.

How much input did Stroud actually have in the hiring of Caley to begin with?

DeMeco Ryans and Nick Caserio spent the offseason publicly declaring Stroud was their guy, while also repeatedly challenging and criticizing him. Yet the reported contract negotiations, including what appeared to be a low initial offer and an unwillingness to accept his counter, painted a somewhat different picture.

And then there's the offensive philosophy itself.

If Stroud is your franchise quarterback, why does it continually feel like the organization is trying to fit him into its preferred offensive identity, with all these New England connections and philosophies, rather than building around what HE does best?

We've seen the blueprint for success when they spread things out, play aggressively and give Stroud answers. Yet they have continually reverted right back to the same issues.

4. And now the damage is already done.

The reluctance to fully trust Stroud and build around his strengths until they were practically forced to has helped put them in this position.

Now they're 3-6, the defense has regressed into the bottom half of the league, and the deficiencies in their coaching, offensive philosophy and roster construction are being exposed.

Meanwhile, the quarterback they chose not to extend is arguably the biggest reason they're even competitive.

And the biggest irony? Stroud's play, despite everything around him, has only strengthened his negotiating position. They could now be looking at a significantly larger contract than what they would've gotten a deal done for this offseason.

And I guess that's ultimately where all of this comes together for me.

If you truly believed in C.J. Stroud as your franchise quarterback the way you've publicly said you do, wouldn't your actions have reflected that?

For one, you would've made a much stronger effort to get him paid and secure his future here before the season.

And two, you would've made sure he had a meaningful voice in choosing the offensive coordinator who would be responsible for his development, and been far more willing, and quicker, to let him help shape the offense around what he does best.

Instead, at least from the outside looking in, it feels like the organization wanted Stroud to fit its vision rather than allowing Stroud to help define that vision.

And only when things started falling apart did they seemingly begin giving him more of that influence.

Now they're sitting at 3-6, with a number of organizational issues being exposed, and a quarterback whose value has only increased despite the circumstances around him.

That's what frustrates me more than anything. It's not just about the losses or the contract. It's the apparent disconnect between how highly this organization says it values Stroud and how much trust they've actually been willing to place in him.

And so much of the mess they're in right now feels self-inflicted.
